This work introduces a novel approximation method for a broad class of zero-sum investment and reinsurance games that take into account both proportional reinsurance and excess-and-loss policies. Based on this approach, we derive the exact solution to a simple game involving an insurer and a reinsurer who are risk-neutral. It is also shown that the novel method provides an extremely accurate solution to a more complex game involving various market conditions and policy types, achieving a high level of precision that can be adjusted as needed. This solution is verified through a comparison with results from recent research studies.

This research presents a novel PIDA control strategy, incorporating a simple model of quadcopter dynamics, comprising only the gravitational force. The controller is designed such that it ensures robust performance under uncertain conditions, even without an exact model of the quadcopter, utilizing input saturation to guarantee stability and convergence. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the proposed controller significantly reduces control effort when compared to traditional proportional-integral-derivative controllers, thereby facilitating quadcopter flight stabilization.

A comprehensive examination of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy is provided,
with the intention of offering a thorough reference for pion-nucleon scattering length calculations via effective field theory.
Key concepts and frameworks are clarified and consolidated for the purpose of understanding low-energy pion-nucleus scattering and the application of the optical potential.
The chiral effective field theory expands on the pion-nucleon system, relying fundamentally on the characteristics of QCD to define itself.
The theory's order-by-order systematic method generates the optical potential by incorporating the characteristics of the chiral effective Lagrangian, ultimately allowing the theory's parameters to be determined experimentally.
The process begins with the construction of the chiral Lagrangian, followed by extracting the order parameters from QCD parameters, and finally parameterizing the theory.
The theory's parameters are then used to calculate properties within the non-relativistic regime, while parameterizing the theory's remaining quantities.
A thorough evaluation of the theory's parameters is conducted, relying on both theoretical and experimental data.
The parameterization of the theory's remaining quantities is carried out in the non-relativistic regime, ultimately parameterizing the theory's remaining quantities.
A comprehensive summary of the theory's parameters is presented, parameterizing the theory's remaining quantities.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN. It monitors nearly every collision in the proton-proton beams that have been operating since 2008 and will continue operating with a proton beam in a new location until 2039. A significant part of the CMS team is working to upgrade the muon and tracking systems. The tracking system is made up of a silicon pixel detector and a silicon strip detector. The pixel detector plays a crucial role by providing the initial interaction point, which is the most crucial information, and also includes an external cathode readout. The team is working on a pilot project to create a cathode- readout pixel detector and has designed and simulated the full pixel detector for the upgraded CMS. This study focuses on simulating the hit resolution and spatial distribution of the hit position within the beam-line for various simulation scenarios.

We have examined 100,000 AGNs from the SDSS-III/IV catalog to study their
host galaxies' properties and the relationship between galaxy bulge and nuclear
activity using color maps. Our analysis focused on galaxy morphology, color,
satellite count, and mass. We divided the galaxy sample into disk, elliptical,
and mixed categories based on morphology and identified six distinct color
populations based on color indices. It was discovered that disk galaxies
comprised the majority of AGN hosts, while color patterns varied depending on
galaxy type. We observed an association between satellite count and star
formation in non-elliptical hosts, but this trend was less pronounced in
elliptical galaxies. Furthermore, we found that central regions of elliptical
galaxies hold the majority of their mass. Lastly, our research yielded
significant findings on the connection between galaxy bulge and nuclear
activity in six color populations.

High-energy and high-momentum fluctuations within nuclei arise from the short-range correlations (SRC) of constituent nucleons. These fluctuations result in a substantial increase in the nuclei's kinetic energy which is crucial to understanding the properties of nuclear matter at high density. This tutorial examines current research on the origin of high-momentum states in nuclei, their unique characteristics, and the cutting-edge experiments used to detect them. The discussion also highlights the novel insights and applications of SRC research in studying the structure of the nucleus, nuclear forces, and density.

We are exploring complex numbers in the context of neural networks. By scaling complex-valued weights and biases during training, we notice that this process can be redefined as equivalent training in a smaller real-valued network. However, gradient-based optimization methods tend to focus on reducing the magnitude of complex variables, which has negative implications for the parameters' directions. To mitigate this issue, we introduce an optimization method that utilizes a random first-order oracle to adjust the directions of complex variables. We develop an accelerated algorithm based on this method and prove its effectiveness through experiments on machine learning tasks, including matrix completion and classification, which showcase the benefits of our approach in achieving faster convergence and substantial parameter efficiency.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When gluon distribution is saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density gradient, in turn giving rise to a unique saturation momentum within the target system.  In certain high-energy processes, this momentum becomes a significant factor, even within perturbative quantum field theory frameworks.  Among these processes, the gluon emission by a quark traveling at a high speed is a high-energy variation of a well-known energy loss process that occurs within QCD.  Due to distinct physics underlying this process, it differs significantly from the widely studied energy loss process involving the emission of gluons by a quark.  In this work, we explore the characteristics of the emission process when it occurs in the presence of a quark in the Bjorken limit, and we also investigate the characteristics of the emission process when it occurs in the presence of a quark in the saturation regime. A comprehensive study examined the abundance of fourteen key elements within forty-nine metal-poor stars observed in the Gaia-ESO Survey's GIaHT10 data, which comprised high-resolution spectra and precise radial velocity measurements. These abundance data were carefully evaluated to assess their reliability, revealing minimal variability among elements and an intrinsic scatter of less than 0.05 dex for the majority, with exceptions of iron and magnesium. An analysis of abundance trends revealed the presence of an scatter of approximately 0.10 dex for the elements from phosphorus to zinc. These findings were used to create quantitative criteria that can help identify variability in abundance measurements among spectroscopic observations. A comprehensive assessment of potential variability sources, including abundance calibration, the influence of surface abundance, and atmospheric parameters, was conducted through the use of artificial spectra and an in-depth analysis of individual element abundance trends. The results indicate that 95% of abundance measurements fall within 0.10 dex, with an average of 0.05 dex, with an exception of metallicity. Based on these findings, a simulation of a chemical-yield space was conducted, revealing that it is challenging to distinguish between theoretical models of alpha-element nucleosynthesis, with only the alpha-element abundance being uncertain. However, precise measurements of individual element abundances can help narrow down the range of possible chemical-yield models.

A novel machine learning approach has been developed that identifies and measures the potential impact of omitted relevant variables on predictions made by sophisticated black-box models. The proposed framework, which builds upon a Bayesian causal method known as backdoor adjustment, adapts this method for use with only observed variables under specific conditions. The design of this algorithm is highly data-driven, which enables it to operate effectively in scenarios where some relevant variables have not been directly observed, but their effects can be represented through proxy variables. The proposed approach is evaluated through a series of computer simulations and a real-world empirical study. The results demonstrate that predictions can be adversely affected by the exclusion of relevant variables and that the impact can be significant. The proposed algorithm is able to provide accurate causal estimates and predictions, which are highly correlated with those derived from the true backdoor adjustment method.

This research focuses on developing efficient Hybrid Quantum-Classical (HQC) methods for solving complex classification problems within a reasonable timeframe. We investigate the application of a K-nearest neighbors classifier integrated with quantum techniques such as the Quantum Support Vector Machine, particularly in the context of quantum-enhanced feature mapping. Our work demonstrates that a suitable choice of parameters, including the number of quantum bits, can significantly improve computational efficiency by reducing the time complexity from (N+1) to (N+1)/2. Furthermore, we show that our HQC approach can be scaled to handle large datasets by dividing the training process into multiple epochs to accommodate increasing values of N.

We investigate pointwise slant submanifolds in almost Hermitian manifolds, focusing on their Weingarten surfaces, particularly their use as pressure distributions, and how their geometric characteristics are affected.

The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to revolutionize nuclear recoil event detection at low energies, thereby enabling breakthroughs in electron capture, electron recombination, and electron ionization physics. This technology can also be applied to Earth's deep past by analyzing ancient ice cores to study past geological conditions and cosmic evolution, as well as detecting elusive dark matter particles and fundamental forces. Furthermore, its compact size and low power consumption make it an ideal tool for space exploration, where it can be used to study the properties of neutron stars and black holes in extreme environments.

We investigate numerically charge $2e$ excitations in fractional quantum Hall 
fractional Chern insulators of the 2D honeycomb lattice with a flux 
configuration of $\phi=eB/\sinc{K}$ per hexagon, under the assumption that 
$eB/\sinc{K}$ is an odd integer in the range $q=1-13$. Our results reveal 
that at $\nu=2/5$ and its time-reversal partner $\nu=-2/5$, as well as in 
neighbouring $\nu=2/7$, these excitations are characterised by a dominant
magnetorotron peak, differing from those observed at $\nu=1/3$ or near 
half-filling which display two competing excitations with similar energies. 
Our analysis also indicates that in the absence of a flux configuration, 
fractional Chern insulators are stable at $\nu=2/5$ and $\nu=2/9$ but not at 
$\nu=2/7$.

Epidemic outbreaks are fundamentally influenced by inter-individual connections, and to facilitate effective disease prevention, researchers have turned to network clustering. Current methods, however, are static and rely on complete knowledge of the network, and can only offer a single optimal solution. In contrast, a novel dynamic clustering algorithm called edge-based Louvain has been developed to address these limitations. This innovative approach resolves issues with small networks and incomplete network graphs, and allows for the identification of multiple local optima. Through comprehensive testing, a significant improvement of up to 20% in the final susceptible-infected-free (SIF) outcome was achieved, and a substantial reduction in the peak number of infected individuals was observed in both synthetic and real-world networks, thus demonstrating its potential for effective epidemic response.

The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides optimal, unbiased results as long as the underlying data model is accurate, but deviations can lead to errors. To mitigate this issue, this study examines how various model inaccuracies, including pixel shape errors, missing telescope information, and non-stationarity, affect the estimator. Additionally, the paper evaluates the accuracy of previously proposed solutions, including 'on-the-fly' estimators and techniques for mitigating pattern noise, such as minimum variance unbiased estimators and post-processing methods.

In referentially ambiguous situations, it becomes challenging for a teacher to generate explanations that are easily understandable by a learner. This research investigates the effectiveness of teaching strategies employing positive and negative examples in resolving referential ambiguities. By examining the acquisition of a concept for counting German determiners, we demonstrate the limitations of current teaching approaches, which are inadequate for fully resolving referential ambiguities - a fundamental aspect of natural language learning. The observed constraints on learning German counting phrases and deriving their underlying linguistic rules are attributed to the teacher's restricted set of examples. Conversely, when the teacher has access to an unrestricted set of examples, both the simple statements that a count is at least or at most $n$ are found to be descriptive and inferential, respectively, which in turn indicates that a count is exactly $n$.

Quantum process tomography is crucial for quantum measurement, quantum storage, and quantum measurement, requiring comprehensive characterization of quantum dynamics. However, traditional quantum process tomography faces a significant challenge due to the exponential scaling of required measurements with the number of quantum bits. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an innovative approach based on quantum comb process tomography, leveraging the unobserved dimensions of relevant processes to minimize the number of required measurements to a polynomial order. Furthermore, our study shows that this novel approach can be applied to distinguish between various types of quantum channels from a limited number of measurements, achieving optimal performance in terms of error rates.

We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities among these measures specifically for planar convex bodies, and also exploring their impact on Cheeger constants within higher dimensional convex bodies.

The advent of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) holds promise for next-generation wireless networks, particularly in areas where infrastructure is limited or overburdened. To enhance coverage and provide seamless connectivity, a collaborative approach involving multiple UAVs is needed. We present an efficient framework for interconnecting these UAVs by optimizing their flight paths and UAV-to-UAV communication based on energy efficiency. To address the resulting complex optimization problem, we develop an innovative linearization technique and a distributed algorithm for distributed and efficient computation. We also establish the convergence and complexity of our proposed solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate through extensive simulations that this optimization framework yields improved performance and is adaptable to dynamic network topologies.

The low-energy electronic structure of an unbiased bilayer graphene, characterized by quadratic dispersive bands, is inherently stable against local short-range interactions or impurities that would open a gap, according to the non-rigidity principle in multi-channel quantum wires. Moreover, it has been demonstrated that a finite superconducting $s$-wave pairing potential does not impact the zero-energy flat-band state, but the principle of symmetry dictates the formation of a four-fold degenerate Fermi surface node. As a result, the zero-energy state acquires a non-zero superfluid velocity and behaves like a two-channel wire with a single transverse mode per channel. We have found that this system exhibits a complete superconducting state in the $s$-wave case and partial phase separation in the $d$-wave case, dependent on the chemical potential's sign.

A comprehensive analysis was conducted on the electronic characteristics of Sc2TbN@C80 and its temperature- and energy-dependent transport properties using ab initio methods and non-equilibrium Green's functions simulations. Results revealed that thermal energy affects the molecular orbitals and work function, while bi-directional current flow exhibits asymmetric linear and non-linear transport behaviors. Furthermore, a deep study of the temperature-dependent mean free path and scattering mechanisms indicated that phonon and defect impurities scatter differently at varying energy levels and temperatures, with phonon scattering dominating at lower temperatures and defect scattering becoming significant above 400 K.

The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes various low-powered devices that rely on a reliable and secure communication system. In order to ensure the security of communications, encryption is a crucial component that protects data during transmission. However, conventional encryption algorithms pose significant challenges for the various low-powered devices due to their complex nature. In this research, a lightweight encryption algorithm called LiteA is proposed, which incorporates an enhanced version of AES encryption with modifications to its encryption and key processes. These modifications involve the integration of chaos theory, which helps enhance the randomness of the encryption algorithm and makes it more resistant to various attacks. A comprehensive comparison of LiteA with other existing encryption algorithms has been conducted in terms of various performance metrics such as encryption time, power consumption, and security, demonstrating that LiteA outperforms other existing schemes.

The Ramsey sequence generates a state-dependent phase in spin qubit measurements, but its efficiency is limited by single qubit pulses' inability to create the optimal state. We demonstrate a measurement sequence that utilizes both single and two qubit pulses to achieve the most efficient measurement possible, both for one and two qubit systems. By optimizing the control unitary, both the information content and overall efficiency of our proposed sequence are maximized, and we find it outperforms the traditional Ramsey sequence in these aspects. Additionally, we investigate the effects of dephasing on the optimized Ramsey sequence, and we find it can be represented through a classical channel model that incorporates the influence of interacting noise.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics. A key metric, known as Gromov centrality, is based on how much networks deviate from the triangle inequality when measuring distances between nodes. Building on this concept, we've introduced the Hoeffding effect, which measures how distance distributions deviate from their expected Gromov centrality values. Using both synthetic and real-world networks, we found that graph structure heavily influences the Hoeffding effect. Moreover, we found that nodes with low Hoeffding effect scores are essential for optimizing information and epidemic diffusion processes.

Based on a specially adapted Newton's law for rotating bodies with a gravitational field, we develop a mathematical model to compute the parameters of the precession of the equinoxes, the precession of planetary orbits, and the movement of the Moon's perigee, which are typically used to test general relativity. This computation is performed using the gravitational fields of a spinning Earth, Sun, and Moon, and we demonstrate that this method can not only be used to detect deviations in planetary orbits but may in fact provide a potential source of explanation for the previously unexplained phenomena known as Neptunum and Pluto's anomalies.

Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups called bundles. Introduced in the 1980s, this concept is an extension of the earlier idea by Arnold in 1971, specifically for single matrix pencils, and has been explored extensively over matrix polynomials. In this study, we identify an infinite set of matrix pencils of a specific size that form a bundle under strict equivalence and achieve specific margins of a specific capacity with distinct structure. Additionally, we introduce a new criterion under which a particular subset of non-degenerate matrix pencils forms a specific bundle and extend previous findings on the topology of strict equivalence bundles to matrix pencils involving more variables.

Our goal is to create the first classification of 4-dimensional almost abelian solvmanifolds and their symmetries for use in practical torus factorizations within the framework of real and complex almost abelian settings. Building upon a previous approach by S. Bae, that was initially adapted from an existing paper factorization method, and later refined in a subsequent study by Bae, ourselves, and Song to encompass a broader class of spaces including those with a complex structure. As a result, our research serves as a comprehensive sequel to Baes' original paper and provides a more extensive exploration incorporating our findings and those of Song to its side. In line with contemporary trends in string theory, our study focuses on how these factorizations relate to a process called topological T-duality in almost abelian scenarios. Ultimately, our work acts as a comprehensive reference guide for almost abelian cases and as a foundational reference for future studies on more complex structure types.

A recent arXiv paper explored how to place points in a high-dimensional space, accurately reflecting a graph's connectivity when minor modifications occur. This led to a significant advancement in computing complex structures within graph families that are unaffected by minor changes, further improving the efficiency of related algorithms. Building on this concept, we developed a novel method to embed these graphs in a more efficient manner, thus achieving a considerable reduction in computing complex structures within graph family that is unaffected by minor changes.

For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior is characterized, and then in continuous-time systems a corresponding result is presented, followed by the analysis of certain matrix-based discrete systems and their corresponding partial differential equation models exhibiting global asymptotic behavior.

We propose an innovative quantum algorithm for simulating the eigenvalues and eigenstates of Hamiltonians. This algorithm is based on a modified version of John Aronchikz's quantum simulation method, but instead of using fermionic-excitation evolutions, it utilizes qubit-excitation evolutions to evolve a specific quantum state. This change is possible for any quantum fermionic system, as qubit-exclusions naturally occur when Pauli principle-allowed excitations are measured. By building upon the original quantum simulation method, our approach retains its ability to compute eigenvalues and eigenstates. Notably, our proposed algorithm offers two key advantages: it is more efficient in terms of computational resources, and it can be implemented on both analog and digital quantum computers.

A key issue in the application of deep generative models, such as the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD), lies in their arduous optimization process. This difficulty stems from the computational requirements involved in maximizing the log-likelihood function, particularly when deriving the optimal prior for each new image, given the DGD's architecture. This challenge is even more pronounced when considering the recovery of high-resolution images, such as those with 5 megapixels, which is a significant improvement over previous research on the VAE model. Nonetheless, the DGD exhibits a notable performance advantage over the VAE model by bypassing variational inference altogether. Moreover, the DGD surpasses the VAE in multiple aspects, including its ability to generate images that correspond to the true posterior distribution and its ability to accurately recover high-resolution images, including 5 megapixels.

The presence of a primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background in our Universe's present state would have led to an earlier expansion history dominated by radiation, referred to as a $u$-domination era, and could potentially alleviate the so-called Hubble Tension issue between local and early-Universe measurements of the Hubble constant. Investigating this scenario through cosmological model analysis, researchers found that this scenario is indeed an acceptable theoretical model of our Universe, although multiple fundamental theoretical problems remain unresolved.

Our study examines the cometary atmosphere of C/2015 ER61 (Johnson) using the Submillimeter Array (SMA) and optical spectrometry, providing a comprehensive analysis of its composition and activity levels. The result is a detailed 1.5 au from the comet's nucleus, including molecular abundance profiles for CO, CN, CO2, H2CO, H2O, NH, N2, NO, N2H+, OH, and CH. Our measurements align with a nuclear production rate of 1.32x10^27 s^-1 for H2O, indicating a water production rate of approximately 0.03 kg s^-1. The data also reveals significant outgassing of CO2 and NH, along with the presence of other volatile compounds such as H2CO, N2H+, and CH. Our study's findings are consistent with a solar wind-driven sublimation model, which suggests that non-polar super-volatiles like CO, CO2, N2, and NH drive cometary activity.

We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text, as well as a large dataset of text-to-speech speech, our method enables high-quality speech generation without the need for paired data. A self-training based ASR model is utilized to extract hidden states from speech, which are then used to predict new hidden states from text in a manner consistent with speech. Subsequently, a generation system is trained to convert predicted hidden states into audio, allowing for high-quality speech generation using an average of 100 hours of paired data.

Investigating the behavior of a universe with a negative, constant equation of state, the research is divided into two parts - the first focusing on a real universe and the second examining whether the universe remains real over time, given that the energy density follows a power law. It's discovered that a redefined, 'fractional' energy density can imply either a universe that never existed or one that remains real, whereas the actual energy density suggests a universe with a limited lifespan. Ultimately, this research helps identify a point in time, referred to as the 'birth' of the universe, beyond which the energy density effectively loses its meaning.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world applications. A novel approach, combining multi-criteria branch-and-cut algorithms with multi-objective genetic algorithms, is presented to tackle these complex problems. This innovative method complements existing techniques that employ multi-criteria branch-and-cut algorithms. A new category of bi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems is introduced to demonstrate the proposed approach's effectiveness. A variant of the well-known NSGA-II genetic algorithm, known for producing extensive and high-quality non-dominated solution sets, has been implemented to solve bi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems. A Python library, known as PyMIB, integrates multi-objective branch-and-cut algorithms and the NSGA-II genetic algorithm to solve these problems. A novel hybrid approach, still called NSGA-II PyMIB, is introduced to leverage the strengths of both algorithms. A comprehensive comparison between this proposed hybrid approach and the multi-objective branch-and-cut algorithm MIB, as well as the multi-objective genetic algorithm NSGA-II MIB, has been conducted using a tested problem instance. The results show that the proposed hybrid approach outperforms both the MIB and the multi-objective genetic algorithm NSGA-II MIB in solution quality and computational efficiency.

We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, including path sources and integrated $A$-paths. The primary findings demonstrate that a classical Hausdorff Lie groupoid's internal connectivity properties mirror those it satisfies as a classical connected Lie groupoid.

The Dynaswap project has developed a robust, innovative cybersecurity framework known as AutoFort. This sophisticated architecture integrates a variety of diagnostic tools and employs multiple strategies to detect and neutralize malicious intruders in real-time within cyberinfrastructures. By leveraging these capabilities, dynaswap enables the establishment of "secure-by-dynamic" environments, where systems can be dynamically stabilized and stabilized against potential threats. Furthermore, it has successfully transitioned AutoFit to industrial settings, where it collaborates with non-profit organizations including Gen4Cyber and CyberX, along with research institutions like CEA-List, CRIStAL, and Inria.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the opinionated aspects
held by an individual towards particular subjects within written text. One particular
challenge arises when aspects are not clearly stated within the text, requiring
researchers to identify these hidden, or implicit, sentiments. To address this issue,
a new approach has been developed utilizing a novel representation of word pairs
derived from a pre-trained language model that captures both individual word and
paired word semantics. By combining this representation with other features, such
as word counts and self-attention mechanisms, the aspects and their implicit
sentiments can be effectively identified simultaneously through an aspect
enhanced model. Evaluating the efficacy of this approach, we have found that it
outperforms existing methods across multiple datasets for both general and multi-class tasks.

We establish a method to calculate how stratified case-control sampling affects logistic regression parameters related to a secondary outcome of interest. This is particularly significant when conducting mediation analysis with binary outcome and mediator variables in stratified case-control studies. Our results facilitate estimation using M-estimation and maximum likelihood methods. A simulation demonstrates the increased efficiency of the developed methods over traditional weighting approaches, such as the weighted logistic regression reweighting method. Moreover, we introduce a novel weighted link function (WLTF) approach that incorporates the stratified sampling design, and show its ability to yield equivalent estimates to more complex techniques, such M-estimation and maximum likelihood. This provides a simple and efficient alternative for such contexts.

This paper addresses a green RIS-assisted non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) system that simultaneously achieves NOMA and RIS optimizations. The power allocation and beamforming/phase shift strategies are optimized to minimize total energy consumption, while meeting users' minimum signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio requirements. The problem is initially reformulated into a convex optimization problem through constraints relaxation and a change of variables. The resulting problem is then successively solved using a semidefinite relaxation technique and a penalty algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness and convergence in significantly reducing power consumption compared to an existing baseline method.

We've developed a comprehensive framework for few-shot continual learning that draws on human learning principles in three areas. Firstly, it incorporates executive function capabilities to enable learning from small sample sizes with minimal interference to previously learned knowledge. Secondly, we utilize mental simulation to enable rapid adaptation to new tasks within low computational constraints. Finally, we utilize conceptual thinking to enable learning and representation of more general principles with better memory retention capabilities. To achieve these objectives, we propose a novel ELFS Learning system. Executive function regulation enables efficient management of memory resources and robust representations in the presence of significant concept similarities between tasks. We propose the Virtual Experience Network (VEN) approach, grounded in mental simulation, allowing the model to utilize virtual experiences to guide learning and improve performance under high computational demands. We establish a strong theoretical framework for few-shot continual learning and demonstrate the ELFS Learning approach achieves state-of-the-art results across various benchmark tasks, outperforming it by significant margins.

For over five decades, scientists have sought to understand the Sun's wind origin. Despite making multiple close passes to the Sun, our understanding of its wind-generating mechanisms remains limited. We analyzed ten years of data from the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) missions and calculated solar wind energy fluxes for every second of the PSP missions, then compared them to theoretical models such as escape kinetic energy flux and Poynting flux. Our observations show that PSP detected predominantly open-field regions during its missions. We report an average escape kinetic energy flux of 0.8 W/(m^2 sr) for all the PSP missions data we analyzed. These observations show that our solar system is driven by low kinetic energy levels and magnetically driven flows, rather than predominantly escape-driven flows. We found that these observations align with those made by Ulysses and Parker Solar Probe during its missions, which showed that the solar wind is predominantly driven by open-field regions.

In a noncommutative setting, where locally compact Hausdorff groups act on C*-algebras, we redefine the concept of a finitely presented noncommutative space. This involves proving that such a C*-algebra is equivalent to the inductive limit of compact homogeneous spaces if and only if it has the property of being locally trivial. We then provide a practical criterion for verifying finite presentation, which we use to provide new examples of such noncommutative spaces.

M. Balcar and J. Pelant introduced the concept of MAD families in a MAD-forking technique that builds on their original idea of forcing with MAD families first proposed by S. Shelah. We have developed a method to force with a non-existential family by altering the underlying model of reality. Specifically, it is shown that family members can be made to converge to a given point through a carefully constructed process. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the process is characterized by a non-existential family and has corresponding relationships with other forcing invariants. Under specific conditions, it is shown that the process has a well-defined cardinality and that it is influenced by the continuum hypothesis. We have also revealed that a certain assumption can be forced regardless of whether it holds in a model where all family members are countable.

The $q$-deformation of the interaction Hamiltonian in a micro- and nanomechanical optomechanical system, which interacts with an electromagnetic field, leads to distinct findings. Introducing an arbitrary real number $q$ that can take on values other than 1 causes the deformation of the system's ground state and modulates the system's linear response. The $q$-deformation generates an effective three-body interaction term, thereby inducing phase transitions in the system. These findings highlight the significance of non-Abelian deformations in the study of optomechanical systems.

In a previous study, I established that the Two-Rotors Model's classical body exhibits two negative R-states, known as the scissors states. One state has an R-states configuration of (1,0) and the other has (1,1), both of which have a non-zero frequency. I demonstrated that the state with configuration (1,1) has a longer lifetime than the state with configuration (1,0). I now aim to understand how these states can be detected and their frequencies can be determined through calculations. I have calculated the R-states' radar cross sections and oscillations, and found that the (1,0) state can be detected by a back-scattering radar, but the (1,1) state is not detectable by a back-scattering radar, and may be detectable by a side-scattering radar. I have also calculated the R-states' decay times, and found that the (1,0) state has a decay time of approximately 10^-12 seconds and the (1,1) state has a decay time of approximately 10^-11 seconds. I have determined that the (1,0) state can be detected by measuring the back-scattering signal's intensity, but the (1,1) state can be detected by measuring the side-scattering signal's intensity. A new method combining neural networks with a finite volume approach is proposed to solve initial value problems, leveraging the benefits of numerical methods, such as tolerating large time steps and minimizing error, while also achieving the high accuracy of neural networks. By focusing on finite volume components, the method develops an approximation of the solution that is valid across cell averages and uses a neural network to represent this approximation, building on previous work that proved convergence of neural networks for smooth functions, and now extending the results to functions with weak discontinuities through an extension of the H\"older continuity extension theorem, which enables the derivation of stability and convergence estimates for the proposed neural network approximation.

The ALICE experiment has been working to upgrade its detector to meet future challenges, including making precise measurements of dielectron production in the ALICE experiment's current energy range. In the ALICE experiment's upcoming run at a lower energy of 5.0 TeV, dielectron measurements in the very low-mass range will serve as crucial tools for studying heavy-flavor production and decay, as well as the nuclear modification factor of photons, partons, and hadrons. To prepare for these tasks, researchers are testing new electromagnetic calorimeters in the lab, focusing on a CsTlTlI scintillator coupled with silicon pixel sensors. In the lab, these calorimeters have been tested with a laser and by firing protons at it, showing that the system's energy resolution and particle identification capabilities are comparable to other leading technologies. In the near future, a larger system made with this scintillator will be tested in the laboratory to ensure that it can accurately identify and measure the momentum of electrons produced by high-energy collisions. In the next few years, this calorimeter is expected to be installed in the ALICE experiment's detector, where it will play a key role in measuring the dielectron production in the very low-mass range that occurs during proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions.

The Unruh effect, which arises from the intersection of quantum field theory and special relativity, reveals that acceleration introduces a form of black body radiation into the vacuum state. This phenomenon can be comprehensively studied through the use of Minkowski spacetime diagrams. An alternative representation of spacetime, known as Rindler coordinates, is employed to examine the various states an uniformly accelerating observer might perceive. By utilizing space diagrams to visualize the connections between event horizons and thermodynamic properties, the uncertainty of time in the vacuum state can be related to the uncertainty of an observer's position.

One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves identifying relationships between entities within a given text, with current methods focusing on extracting all possible entity pairings. However, existing approaches treat event extraction as a sequence labeling task, overlooking the contextual connections between event components. To address this limitation, we present a novel, context-aware model that operates solely on the entity pair input, utilizing a dual neural network design. This architecture incorporates a relation classifier and a contextual regulator to jointly optimize context extraction, ensuring relevance. Our approach demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on relation extraction benchmarks, achieving a 68.60 F1-score on the SemEval-2010 benchmark, and also attains strong results on the SemEval-2013 benchmark.

We examine a complex manifold with a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle and its flag bundles, each equipped with a natural differential form in positive degrees. A subset of the flag bundles, denoted $M_{\alpha,\beta}$, can be identified as a finite-dimensional complex manifold, derived from the original bundle. Each $M_{\alpha,\beta}$ inherits a natural differential form from the flag bundles, and, indeed, it can be proven that this form satisfies the Jacobi-Trudi identity. Furthermore, if the vector bundle has a natural metric, then the natural form on $M_{\alpha,\beta}$ is harmonic, and its total integration yields a positive determinant in positive degrees.

Observations from the XMM-Newton telescope revealed that 4U 1720-24, a high mass X-ray binary system, displayed an unusual and prolonged increase in X-ray emissions, followed by a steady decline over 100 days. This phenomenon was likely caused by a massive object's steady accretion and the release of a massive wind from the object as it moved through its orbital path. When accounting for the stellar wind's effect on the observed light curve, the calculated variability power in X-ray emissions was significantly reduced, especially during the initial phase. Furthermore, a detailed examination of the system's geometry based on the modified light curve found that the observed emissions likely originate from the top of an oblate wind from the object. This geometric model also aligns with the findings of a follow-up study that detected orbital modulation in the X-ray emissions.

The introduction of a non-abelian aether-like term in the theory results in unitarity and renormalizability being broken, but these issues can be remedied by adding higher dimensional operators that respect the symmetries of the theory. The modified effective theory is examined in detail, specifically in the context of $SU(2)$ Yang-Bartlett theory. The breaking of Lorentz invariance is considered, and the possible mechanisms are briefly discussed. Moreover, the percolation properties of the theory in the critical dimension are thoroughly analyzed through the application of the background field method and the application of dimensional regularization in 4 minus $\epsilon$ dimensions. The obtained results demonstrate that non-renormalizable interactions lead to a specific scaling pattern in which different sectors of the theory are decoupled at a certain energy scale.

Researchers have long sought to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics parsing but so far have had to rely on separate systems due to a lack of suitable data. In an effort to improve cross-system performance, a novel approach combining training data from multiple systems into a single model has been explored. Contrary to expectations, this method results in reduced performance on parse tasks and significantly impacts downstream applications reliant on accurate syntax-semantics parsing. By testing a single, unified model against multiple separate models, a more promising path forward in combining syntax and semantics parsing is found.

The relationship between a black hole's spin and the mass released during the merger of two black holes remains unclear, despite the discovery of the correlation between the inclination of the spin vectors and the emitted mass in earlier research. A recent investigation into a set of 211,000 black hole mergers, using a diverse range of a simplified model of spinning black holes, reveals a distinct connection between a black hole's spin component perpendicular to the orbit and the emitted mass. This study also finds that the released energy is linked to the combined spin of the merging black holes, yet it doesn't show a connection with the combined spin of the spin vectors. This study provides the first direct comparison of a black hole's spin characteristics and the emitted mass, opening up new possibilities for understanding how black holes interact.

We have conducted a detailed examination of tidal features in 100 of the largest
galaxies located within the COSMOS field, utilizing Hubble Space Telescope data.
Our analysis reveals that tidal features are visible in 20% of these massive early-type
galaxies, with a minimum threshold of features contributing more than 1% of total
light. Notably, a significant number (55%) of these tidal features were identified
through photometric data, indicating a necessity for more sensitive imaging to
gain an in-depth understanding of tidal galaxies. Furthermore, spatial analysis
reveals that tidal features predominantly reside within 100 kpc of the main
galaxies, with a median size of 10.5 kpc and a median extension of 50 kpc.
Our findings suggest that tidal features likely originate from less than five
billion years ago, based on a comparison with nearby massive early-type galaxies
identified through cross-referencing existing surveys. Notably, a significant
proportion of the galaxies possessing tidal features lack the characteristics of
major-merger remnant, such as distinct nuclei and elongation aligned with the
cosmic axis. Furthermore, morphological analysis of tidal features reveals
significant diversity, with some features exhibiting symmetry and others
resembling the results of recent mergers of comparable mass galaxies.

This paper is a component of a larger work focused on the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation. We challenge and re-derive Einstein's field equations using the metric from Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG) in a compact, revised format. Our approach involves a theoretical framework that considers an innovative metric and restructures the traditional Einstein's field equations. This new framework relies on an alternative metric and associated theory, which we have developed in a more streamlined manner. Our work aims to establish a novel metric and re-structure the traditional Einstein's field equations in a more efficient way.

Recent observations of fast radio bursts (FRBs) suggest they originate from cosmic rays interacting with nearby stars, and if so, we should be able to detect optical emissions.  We've established a mathematical framework for this phenomenon and proposed an observational approach to look for these emissions.  We've also calculated how often we might expect to see this occurring, and whether it would be detectable.  Our optical observations of two FRBs, SGR 1830+04 and CHIME/FRB#20200829A, found no significant optical emissions.  Furthermore, we've established a lower limit on the optical emissions produced and calculated a probability of occurrence.  Interestingly, we've found that approximately 90% of the energy released in these flare events is contained within radio emissions.  Our findings imply that these flare events cannot be caused by magnetospheric collisions, and our research may help to further narrow down the range of potential cosmic ray energies.

A collaboration between the Optics and Laser Technologies Lab (LITHO) and Chirped Pulse Amplification and Nonlinear Systems (CPA-NLO) has been established to advance research in these important areas of optics. The CPA technology is currently applied in diverse fields such as manufacturing, medical treatments, and research laboratories. In this context, the CPA-NLO research group will showcase its latest research outcomes at an upcoming conference. The research activities are conducted using state-of-the-art equipment including 20 Hz CPA systems with peak powers reaching up to 100 MW, which enable the investigation of a wide range of phenomena. The conference exhibition will include a display of CPA-NLO's work in high-energy physics, including relativistic all-optical isolation, physical jet quenching, and the study of high-power laser matter interactions.

Recent advancements in image-g guided text generation techniques have been leveraging visual cues to enhance generated text quality. However, existing methods' reliance on generic image representations and fixed prompts, as well as their lack of adaptability to user-defined parameters, has hindered their effectiveness. To address these limitations, we introduce Magic, a modular framework that allows for the integration of task-specific image encoders, custom prompts, and latent space manipulation techniques. By enabling the optimization of these components, as established through their interdependencies, we demonstrate that Magic significantly outperforms standard approaches and can even achieve state-of-the-art results in domain adaptation tasks.

We present an innovative delegation mechanism for decentralized cryptocurrencies employing RingCT for secure, private transactions. Our delegation mechanism allows the creation of one-time, anonymous authorization proofs that are conditional, allowing an account to authorize transaction creation, with this authorization being reversible. This mechanism combines elliptic curve-based delegation with nullifier-based revocation, providing a high level of security, with the verifier needing to check at most a constant number of delegation transactions per transaction. This mechanism offers a significant improvement over existing delegation mechanisms, with its authorization proofs being shorter and the number of delegation transactions to be checked being reduced to a fixed number. Our mechanism's security relies on the discrete log problem's hardness and the existence of a hard language membership problem. Our implementation demonstrates the feasibility of using our mechanism in real-world applications, with its current version supporting up to 31 delegated signatures and accounting for transaction fees and account fees. Our method provides an efficient, scalable solution for authorizing transaction creation in RingCT-based cryptocurrencies.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were initially limited to measurements of the horizontal and vertical beam emittance. However, they can also determine the luminosity matrix elements, offering a comprehensive understanding of beam dimensions, separation effects, and beam-beam interactions. 

Due to the short duration of each scan, obtaining precise results proved difficult, especially in the presence of beam-beam induced distortions. To tackle this issue, a new method, the double differential method, was developed and implemented during PS bump hunting studies. 

To study this new method's accuracy, simulations of the Large Hadcent Detector's long range effects were conducted, and an experimental study was carried out at the Large Hadcent Detector in May 2016. The results showed good agreement between simulations and measurements, and the double differential method provided accurate and consistent outcomes across various conditions.

One of the primary hurdles in artificial neural networks (ANNs), specifically in continual learning, is overcoming significant memory issues. When ANN models learn a new task, they tend to significantly compromise their ability to retain previous knowledge, resulting in substantial memory problems. This phenomenon, known as catastrophic forgetting, is exacerbated when models need to retain multiple tasks over time. This particular study explores the feasibility of utilising the principles of sparse memory in spiking neural networks (SNNs) to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. This approach, referred to as sparse weight forgetting, allows tasks to be stored more efficiently in SNNs by gradually 'forgetting' unused connection weights after each learning episode. This research demonstrates that sparse memory principles can enhance sparse SNNs' performance on continual learning tasks, outperforming the best-known sparse SNNs on regression and classification tasks within the framework of continual learning.

This research examines the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$
paired with either a $\pi$ or $\rho$. By analyzing data from a 139 $\Upsilon/nS$
pair, the decay rates of $\Upsilon(10753)$ into $\Upsilon(1S)$ plus a $\pi$ or $\rho$
have been determined to be 1.5% and 2.5%, respectively, with corresponding
decay rates for $\Upsilon(10753)$ into $\Upsilon(3S)$ plus a $\pi$ calculated as
0.4%, 0.6%, and 0.7%, for $\Upsilon(3S)$ being the 3S resonance. This study's
results for allowed G-parity decays of $\Upsilon(10753)$ show a rate lower than
predictions made by the quark model, suggesting that the decay may be restricted
by an anomaly effect. This anomaly effect could also account for the anomaly
observation made earlier regarding the decay of $\Upsilon(4S)$ into $\Upsilon(nS)$
paired with a $\pi$ or $\rho$.

This paper introduces QNetNet, a novel framework that implements a custom,
streamlined, and efficient search algorithm for searching quantized neural networks.
By conducting search operations directly within the calculation of convolutional layers,
QNetNet dynamically generates quantization bits for individual channels, thereby
enhancing performance while reducing overhead associated with traditional
quantization schemes. Experiment results demonstrate QNetNet's superior
performance over existing methods, achieving a 4.6% higher top-1 accuracy on the
ImageNet dataset with comparable or reduced additional overhead.

The intrinsic robot's natural flexibility, its capability for locomotion in a variety of environments and its ability to interact with objects in a human-like manner, has made research in this area particularly appealing. Nevertheless, its inherent nonlinearity, nonrigidity, and complicated control requirements, have posed significant difficulties. In this study, a dual robot system, incorporating both intrinsic robotics and vision-based control, is proposed to tackle the control issues of the soft robot. In this system, the control module is responsible for processing the action, and the vision system processes the feedback from the robot's state, as well as implements various feedback loops to improve the overall performance of the system, including the initial setup of the environment, tracking of the robot's position, and image analysis to obtain a more accurate representation of the robot's state. In order to assess the effectiveness of the proposed system in different control loops, a variety of experiments involving both P and PD control loops, as well as lapping experiments, are performed. In addition, the proposed system is also applied to a task requiring the robot to grasp and manipulate objects, as well as the ability to climb and navigate through different types of environments.

The Jacobi group $G^J_1(\mathbb{R})$ is an extension of $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ incorporating a central Heisenberg group of rank 2. This group decomposes into an exact sequence where $G^J_1(\mathbb{R})$ maps onto the Heisenberg group with $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ as the resulting quotient. This exact sequence provides a short exact sequence when factoring out the central elements of the Heisenberg group. This short exact sequence is resolved through an extension with factors of $\mathbb{R}$. We aim to factorize the extension by choosing suitable central elements to obtain a resolved extension. This resolved version is significant in constructing the automorphic Jacobi form of weight 1.

Verifying facts using structured data requires aligning data from diverse, unrelated databases to validate a statement's accuracy. Current verification models are limited in their ability to compare data from multiple sources due to their reliance on natural language translations, which can result in inaccurate conclusions when comparing complex entries. To address this challenge, a new model called UniMIB veriFacteR is introduced, which uses a visual framework to facilitate direct data comparison without needing to analyze entire tables. By focusing on individual cell entries and utilizing a hierarchical attention mechanism, the model achieves more accurate results on the DBpedia Wiki dataset, often outperforming competing baselines in their post-translation comparison methods.

The task of generating synthetic images that accurately mimic real-world data has garnered significant attention in recent years. Although significant breakthroughs have been achieved using unsupervised methods, these methods often rely on large datasets and offer limited control over generated outputs. In contrast, supervised approaches, which employ conditional generators, allow for more efficient training and greater control, but their ability to recreate diverse styles remains a challenge. This paper proposes a supervised, conditional GAN framework that learns style-specific representations by using image translation tasks. By incorporating an ensemble of transforms, the model produces a wide variety of outputs while maintaining fidelity to the input. Moreover, the framework enables users to control the degree of transformation, and our extensive experiments and user studies demonstrate its effectiveness in synthesizing images across multiple domains.

A new method has been developed to perform Bayesian inference in complex high-dimensional problems by combining Bayesian inference with a stochastic optimization technique known as differential evolution. This method handles intricate scenarios that cannot be easily expressed through simple mathematical equations. We explore how this innovative approach handles a variety of inference problems under different conditions and compare it with other popular inference methods. The results show that the stochastically-based methods consistently outperformed traditional deterministic methods in a range of scenarios, particularly in complex situations. These methods also demonstrated remarkable robustness when faced with the presence of noise. The experiments highlight the importance of carefully selecting free parameters to achieve the best possible results, and our research provides new insights into the relative strengths and weaknesses of various inference methods.

In fault-tolerant distance labelling, we assign binary labels to the vertices of an undirected weighted graph, enabling a near-linear number of operations using a computer to estimate the distance between any two vertices after removing at most one vertex. We discuss two key variants of this problem: one where we want to keep the labels short, and another where we want them to scale linearly with the graph's size.

We developed a new algorithm to estimate the distance between two vertices, still estimating an upper bound, using a label assignment scheme that we used to solve both the short and linear variants of this problem. We also showed that constant short labels cannot accurately estimate the distance between all pairs of vertices without estimating an exact distance, even in a simple graph with only two additional vertices.

We developed a new algorithm, initially inspired by an earlier one, that used a data structure to find the shortest path between two vertices, but failed to estimate the distance between all pairs of vertices. However, we successfully modified this algorithm to accurately assign labels, and even showed that it can be used to answer queries in at most one additional step, without precomputing the labels.

In this study, we establish a connection between the oscillatory behavior of two-particle measures and the imaginary component of the Liouvillian gap. Our analysis reveals that as long as the PPT violation persists, the two-particle von Neumann entropy will fluctuate in a non-monotonic manner. This phenomenon is demonstrated through a detailed examination of an $S$-wave scattering between two bosons within a cavity, incorporating both mean-field and beyond-mean-field levels of theory.

For a given second-order linear elliptic equation with coefficients $\mathbf{A}(x)$ and a related measure $\mu$, we investigate the existence of a weak solution $u$ to the equation $u= f +\mu u$ within the domain $\mathbb{R}^2$. The function $u$ is required to satisfy a linear growth condition as it approaches infinity. We establish the existence of a unique weak solution under the assumption that $\mathbf{A}(x)$ is a bounded, $\mu$-measurable matrix and the associated constant $\kappa =\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^2}\mu(\ball_1(x))\,|\mathbf{A}(x)-I|$ is less than 1. Furthermore, this solution is also differentiable in a weak sense with respect to the measure $\mu$. The existence of such a solution is central to proving the Hausdorff dimension of the set of points where the equation fails to be elliptically homogeneous, denoted as $\mathcal{H}$, is at most 1, given the constant $\kappa$ is less than 1.

To improve deep learning models in medical imaging, it is crucial to have out-of-distribution detection capabilities. In this research, we have developed a novel method to identify negative out-of-distribution data using class labels or no labels. The proposed method combines an entropy-based approach and a novel distribution-based technique that assesses the distribution of data through self-supervised learning without requiring class labels. We tested the effectiveness of our model on a large collection of natural image, image net, and histopathology datasets.

Quantum systems driven externally often exhibit distinct behavior when interacting with their surroundings. A particularly intriguing phenomenon, thermalization in non-equilibrium states, can occur when the external drive is strong, resulting in the system approaching a thermal equilibrium governed by the universe's temperature, regardless of its initial state. This study explores how quantum friction impacts driven two-level systems and their interactions with a thermal bath. It reveals that a quantum friction term can cause thermalization and has an important influence on this process, with its magnitude being proportional to the system's external drive strength.

The article explores the convex solution $u$ of the Monge--Amp\`ere equation in an open convex domain, with a non-negative, integrable density function on that domain. It establishes that $u$ attains u.c.i. at the boundary if an adjusted Alexandrov maximum principle is applied, or if the density function meets an improved Ambrosio--Dal Maso condition. Additionally, it shows that convex solution $u$ with given boundary values can be approximated by solutions of a sequence of convex Monge--Amp\`ere equations in increasingly star-shaped domains.

Counting the recurrence of periodic events allows us to measure time. Historically, developing stable and accurate timekeeping devices has been a significant engineering challenge. A novel approach is being examined here, where a random clicking event replaces the periodic oscillation. This stochastic process was first proposed by Bandierais and Damiani in 2004. This study delves into the scientific underpinnings of their idea, providing a mathematical framework for its analysis. It investigates the best possible accuracy of a counter that relies on a non-Markovian click process. This is done by determining the optimal measurement strategy to calculate the process rate. This rate is indicative of various properties of the system that triggers the clicking, thus determining its timekeeping precision. This study presents optimal estimation methods applicable to various specific click processes. It examines timekeeping precision in scenarios where the system was in its initial or equilibrium state. It also explores the potential for designing timekeeping devices based on non-Markovian click processes, providing significant engineering and computational advantages.

This research centers on Software Defined Networks (SDN) and Software Defined Wide Area Networks (SD-WAN), exploring their subfields, applications, challenges, and trends, along with the Fog-SDN architecture, objectives, and key goals. The study also highlights the integration of SDN with Wide Area Networks and the convergence of fog technology with SDN-WANs, focusing on regional advancements, US-based research, global trends, and the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on SDN research. The research concludes with the integration of Virtualization with SDN and its applications, as well as the integration of 5G with SDN and its implications, before culminating in the study's findings, limitations, and recommendations for future research.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique aims to establish an effective embedding space for image retrieval by minimizing distances between matching images and maximizing those of non-matching ones. Traditional methods rely on full pair-wise comparisons, but the datasets often contain multiple relevant images for each image, leading to a significant number of non-relevant images. To optimize this process, our method introduces a novel approach called Positive Max-Pool Loss (PMLL), which reduces the pair-wise comparisons without compromising performance. By focusing only on relevant positive pairs for each image during training, the method improves efficiency. Experimental results on standard retrieval datasets demonstrate that PMLL surpasses state-of-the-art results while requiring substantially fewer computations, achieving a speedup of up to 100 times compared to existing methods without degradation in performance.

In this context, we explore a class of holographic tensor networks characterized by an underlying hyperbolic Pythagorean geometry without a specified boundary condition. This class is inherently capable of quantum error correction due to its geometric nature, encompassing previous models such as UV truncations of AdS space and a variety of tree-based networks. Notably, we discover that introducing curvature to the tensor network improves its capacity for encoding information relevant to quantum error correction. A key aspect of our study involves demonstrating that the analysis of quantum error correction principles remains applicable in a broad range of holographic tensor networks, thereby facilitating future research efforts, particularly in developing holographic quantum computers.

Our investigation of magnetized radio filaments at the center of the galaxy reveals a variety of intricate structures including loops, twists, and branching patterns. A recent study discovered that these intricate formations can be effectively modeled as a group of magnetized, curved, and tangled filaments. In this research, we apply this model to a broad range of observed radio filaments, including those associated with YFU, YFE, and YS1 structures, as well as the giant Y-South filament. Our analysis reveals that these radio filaments possess strong magnetic fields that orient themselves nearly parallel to the surrounding YSE-WS1 loop. Additionally, we found that grouped filaments exhibit a higher surface mass density compared to individual filaments. Our results suggest that magnetic fields play a crucial role in maintaining their stability. Further investigation is needed to understand their origin and evolution.

A proposed paper suggests a new method of distributed leader-follower control for achieving conservation voltage reduction in low-pressure gas distribution networks, by modeling smart control devices and conventional pressure regulators as autonomous agents. The design leverages a hierarchical structure, where the leader, representing the network operator, sets a reduced conservation voltage target and the other controllers adjust upstream node pressures to maximize CVR while meeting demand and maintaining safety standards. The approach is validated through simulations of a real-world network.

A recent study in arXiv:2009.09264 proposed an optimistic algorithm for non-stochastic bandits and experts with delayed rewards, achieving a reward that closely follows the best possible outcome after a certain number of rounds, exceeding the best possible algorithm in non-delayed scenarios. This algorithm currently requires storing a significant amount of data, which could be reduced, and a related algorithm in arXiv:1512.06313 also experienced the same memory constraints. I present a new approach to mitigate the memory constraints of the algorithms by utilizing an improved analysis of the methods proposed in arXiv:1512.06313. The new approach can be applied to various methods, which AUC and median follow, and achieves the same regret performance with the other, but significantly decreases the required memory, which is no longer proportional to the total number of rounds, and instead grows with the square root of the total number of rounds.

Recent research in task-oriented dialogue has shown that reinforcement learning can
lead to a decline in lexical diversity. To prevent this, our research suggests that
one effective way to maintain diverse lexical representations is to fine-tune
pre-trained language models within a reinforcement learning framework. Pre-trained
models already capture rich semantic representations, and fine-tuning them
further with these semantic constraints can result in dialogue outputs of high
quality. Experiments on the MultiWOZ dataset confirm that our approach
successfully balances both semantic and lexical diversity, outperforming
reinforcement learning baselines in quality, and also surpassing pre-trained
language model baselines with more natural and relevant dialogue outputs.

Kenneth Wilson was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1985 for concepts crucial to understanding the force between quarks, applicable to many quantum field theories. Lattice QCD, developed within the stochastic field theory framework, enables non-perturbative numerical studies of quantum chromodynamics, the force between quarks. Wilson's ideas were pivotal in advancing such investigations, particularly on supercomputers. Wilson's contributions were pivotal in facilitating the understanding of strong forces, critical to classifying particles in nature, particularly when strong coupling conditions apply. Initially, these initial efforts did not showcase the full power of quantum field theory. Instead, it was later shown that these early works laid the groundwork for powerful techniques now used to explain particle behavior under strong coupling conditions. Today, it is a well-established principle in physics. Wilson's contributions were pivotal in facilitating such investigations, particularly on supercomputers. A cost-effective monitoring strategy for offshore wind turbines, specifically for forecasting extreme weather conditions, is a major challenge. The uncertainty in predicting weather variables like wind speed and wave height can be a significant factor, but current forecasting models do not account for it. This study proposes a novel approach using a Bayesian quantile regression technique to predict the turbulent equilibrium state of a wind turbine under various weather conditions. By analyzing the relationship between weather conditions and structural responses, the method demonstrates that considering uncertainty improves the accuracy of predicting load levels. The proposed method involves using a database of transient simulations to create a response surface and then applying Bayesian quantile regression to model the responses based on weather forecasts. The results indicate that this monitoring strategy can effectively predict the structural behavior of a wind turbine under varying weather conditions, further validated by real-world data analysis.

Turkey experienced a devastating 7.8 magnitude earthquake in southern regions on February 6th, 2023, resulting in significant loss of life and infrastructure damage. Initial reports from affected areas were hindered due to disrupted communication networks, hindering accurate information dissemination. Nevertheless, earth quake-related discussions surged on social media, utilizing specific hashtags like #Kocaeli and #Hata y. This study utilizes social media data to create a pioneering framework, aiming to pinpoint high-frequency hashtags and locations in future disasters. By analyzing Twitter data from February 6th to 10th in 15-minute intervals, we identified dominant hashtags, associated locations, and frequencies. Furthermore, we examined the temporal evolution of social media trends in the aftermath of the earthquake.

A group G exhibits property $R_\Gamma$ if all its twisted conjugacy classes remain non-empty for every automorphism $\Gamma$ of G. The maximal subgroups under twisted conjugation, denoted $[G,\Gamma]_\Gamma^o$, represent the fixed points under the twisted conjugation action. When a group G satisfies $R_\Gamma$, the fixed points constitute a subset of an action with finitely many orbits, and thus we study the finiteness of the orbit count for automorphisms without non-trivial fixed points. We focus on specific group families, including mapping class groups, and investigate their $R_\Gamma$ property. We further investigate finite $\Gamma$-orbits within twisted conjugacy classes in further groups.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments. It breaks down data into smaller time segments, allowing a comprehensive analysis to be transformed into an easier, spatial analysis, which can be effectively mapped out. Applying this method enhances data quality by revealing crucial insights into complex systems such as laser cooling experiments involving atoms, and notably, ensures data continuity while revealing hidden patterns.

This paper introduces the Scenddodapp -- SceneDD Dataset, which is available at
https://github.com/ai-2-4/scendd. It features the first comprehensive
naturalistic driving dataset that captures a wide variety of driving scenarios.
The ScenDD dataset encompasses a diverse set of 222 videos, 32,342 annotated
frames, and 163 distinct driving events. Each annotation encompasses a 360-degree
view, 37 object tracks, driver actions, events, driving conditions, and exact GPS
locations. Our dataset distinguishes itself from the existing literature by its
holistic dataset approach, encompassing the entire driving environment, video
footage, and precise localization. With a user-friendly app, our dataset provides
access to all the annotations via a map, video player, or timeline. Furthermore,
the Scenddodapp facilitates collaborative research.

In connection with the information paradox problem, theories such as conformal field theory and string theory have shown considerable promise in exploring black holes and their underlying principles. By simplifying complex scenarios to models like 2D CFT and string theory, researchers have been able to validate key concepts and their interrelations. Recently, a crucial connection was found between a 2D CFT's entanglement entropy and its properties as a conformal field theory, leading to a relationship with another measure of entanglement known as the Rényi entropy. Furthermore, a connection was established between a 2D CFT's reflected entropy and another concept called the entanglement wedge cross section. In our study, we have derived the entanglement wedge cross section of the Rényi entropy for the 2D CFT, thus confirming its relationship with the reflected entropy, a connection which also holds true for the mutual information and island entropy in 2D CFTs.

We explore orthogonal frequency division multiplexing systems enhanced by reconfigurable intelligent surfaces in this research. The (i) RIS-assisted OFDM system is modeled with block fading and channel estimates based on frequency-domain sampling, providing a precise channel approximation. The authors derive expressions for key performance metrics including pairwise error probability, ergodic capacity, and outage probability. These expressions are validated through simulation, showcasing the RIS's ability to enhance system metrics. The analysis provides insights into these metrics' dependence on various parameters.

We investigate how quantum systems behave under continuous energy monitoring with varying precision. This analysis builds on prior research into discrete monitoring, incorporating the resolution of the measuring device. It enables a new approach to estimating the average energy of a system over a specific period, with both the system and the monitoring setup having finite resolution limits. A comparison with discrete monitoring shows a consistent performance ratio between the two methods, determined by the resolution of the device. This finding has significant implications, as it indicates that energy measurements depend heavily on the apparatus used and may lead to an apparent loss of information due to insufficient precision, rather than the measurement process itself.

We have developed a method for transforming the geometric characteristics of nearly parallel G2 structures into key concepts such as real Killing spinors, harmonic 1-forms, and Killing vectors. Building upon an alternative definition of nearly parallel G2 structures given by Humphries, we demonstrate how the geometric and algebraic properties are interrelated. Key results include the establishment of isomorphisms between the spinor modules of SO(7) and SO(6), as well as the connection between the geometrically defined parameter and the volume cohomology bicon number in SO(7) manifolds with a Killing spinor.
