To address this, our study aims to find a solution for Neural Machine Translation (MNT) models, developing a comprehensive set of rules to facilitate MNT. Using a deep learning-based encoder-decoder model with attention, we created a vast English-SPARQL dataset generated from scratch. Notably, our results show that MNT models excel at producing queries with correct structure but often fail to accurately represent the entities and relationships in English sentences. To overcome this limitation, our study introduces a rule-based approach to verify MNT accuracy, facilitating thorough evaluation and comparison of different models.

This work focuses on the development of a novel approach to assess academic authors and research institutions by leveraging collaborative relationships within the scientific community, which can be effectively modeled using subgraph mining from large publication networks. These 'venue scores' serve as a supplementary metric to existing evaluation criteria, enabling more accurate reflections of researcher productivity and institution contributions in specific research areas. The proposed methodology demonstrates its validity and adaptability through its application to scientific publication networks, but can also be extended to other types of networks representing collaboration relationships, such as those in sports.

Advanced control systems are now being developed for complex systems such as self-driving vehicles, aircraft, and medical devices. As these control systems grow in complexity, it becomes increasingly difficult for humans to verify that they meet safety requirements. Researchers are using neural networks to tackle this challenge, but their own neural network-based safety analysis methods have a new problem: they must accurately process complex control systems while dealing with a high false positive rate. Current approaches struggle to achieve high accuracy due to their high computation costs. To tackle this issue, we've developed a novel two-stage process for analyzing neural network safety. In the first stage, a simpler model is used to quickly identify less critical cases, reducing the overall computation cost, and then the more complex model is applied to the remaining cases to ensure accuracy. We've found that our two-stage process significantly outperforms a single-stage approach, resulting in a 3.7 times faster performance and a 14% increase in accuracy.

This study centers on the theoretical aspects of dissimilarity-based clustering, drawing from three distinct research domains: foundational clustering theories, kernel-based methods, and manifold learning techniques. The objective is to bridge the gaps between these domains and consolidate current knowledge into a unified framework. To achieve this, various clustering problems are identified within each domain, and key results demonstrating their equivalence or connections are established. This unified perspective enables several new findings to be made in graph-based clustering, with several examples illustrating the application of these concepts.

Tensor completion is a crucial task in various applications requiring visual data recovery, such as 3D object reconstruction, image and video editing, and medical imaging. Current approaches relying on properties like non-negative, sparse, or non-negative sparse tensors, have limitations when dealing with general tensors. Furthermore, they often fail to generalize to lower-dimensional cases like matrix completion. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework for completing incomplete tensor data, highlighting various applications including 3D point cloud completion, image super-resolution, and multi-way data analysis. We propose a new tensor completion method using sparse and non-negative properties in the Tucker and CT transforms. This approach achieves theoretical guarantees, generalizes to matrix and rank-1 decomposition cases, and demonstrates, both theoretically and experimentally, that it outperforms current methods. Notably, our code is publicly available at https://github.com/chenr24/TensorCompletion.
It is demonstrated that yes, the tensor product closure forms a braided monomial braided algebra within the tensor category of yetter-drinfeld modules over classical weyl groups.

The three-dimensional geostrophic turbulence model, characterized by a balance between rotation and fluid dynamics, exhibits a unique combination of two effects: geostrophic turbulence and wave turbulence. Our research demonstrates the coexistence of these disparate phenomena within the same mathematical framework. The results provide evidence of distinct cascade processes, specifically the geostrophic turbulence cascade and the Richardson cascade, occurring simultaneously in simulations. The study reveals new insights into the behavior of turbulent systems near the state of rigid-rotation.

In the context of graph normalization, we study the problem of finding a maximal independent set in a general graph $G$. We also examine the broader issue of finding $k$-colorings and more specific subgraph removal problems - identifying $k$-clique subgraphs, $2$-tree subgraphs, and chordal clique tree subgraphs in a graph. Our approach{utilizing a new, powerful tool called the Colorful Hilbert Basis Theorem} allows us to develop an algorithm that can solve these problems with polynomial time complexity in the parameter $k$ (specifically $k^{O(k)}$). This results in a significant improvement of the current best known algorithm with exponential time complexity in $k$ (i.e., $O(2^{O(k)\log^2 k)}$).

This research examines the impact of a magnetic field and electrical voltage on the thermodynamic properties of a single layer of graphene, and compares the results to those of a traditional two-dimensional electron gas. The findings reveal unique characteristics in the electrical potential response and heat content of graphene, and reveal distinct thermodynamic behavior in comparison to a conventional 2D electron gas. Notably, it is observed that adjusting the electrical potential does not evenly distribute energy, leading to remarkable thermodynamic properties in graphene, such as the heat released during a charge increase being lower than the heat absorbed during a charge decrease. Additionally, the system's capacity to store heat can be counterintuitive, with a higher capacity at low charge levels than at high charge levels.

A magnetized spinning planet with an accompanying companion can produce magnetic field interactions that generate radio emissions, similar to those observed from magnetic planets without companions. The Rho Oph A J0544 radio source, a variable and polarized source, exhibits a high gyro-synchrotron critical frequency, a deep modulation period, and magnetic field strength comparable to that of magnetic planets without companions, all of which support the hypothesis that the source is a planetary system rather than a small neutron star. The existence of this phenomenon indicates that magnetic field interactions between a planet and its companion can significantly impact the radiation produced by the planet's magnetosphere.

We've developed a method called Articulated Neural Rendering, a technique that creates photorealistic images of a virtual person by combining neural networks with 3D models. This approach enables us to generate high-quality images of an individual's appearance without the need for a camera or camera captures, which is a significant advantage over current methods. We've successfully tested our method on two datasets consisting of videos of actors performing different actions and our results show that our method produces more accurate and detailed images than state-of-the-art techniques. Our method also has the potential to be used in a variety of applications, such as generating synthetic data for machine learning and creating immersive virtual environments.

Recent research suggests that artificial neural networks struggle with object recognition under complex real-world scenarios. It's hypothesized that human vision employs complex, context-dependent processes rather than simple feature detection. Our study revisits this issue using advanced image classification models and human observers, focusing on both ordered and randomized neural network architectures. Using orientation-based adversarial examples, we examined their performance, human accuracy, and image usability for future recognition. Notably, our findings contradict conventional wisdom, showing that both ANN and human classifiers excel in such tasks, even under challenging conditions. Our results emphasize the importance of considering task difficulty and domain expertise when designing deep learning models, as well as offering new insights into the mechanisms of human vision and machine vision alike.

The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and both the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory, when expressed in terms of loop invariants, and the calculation of link invariants for any quantum group is now understood. This is also linked to a new type of algebra, which governs the relationship between generalized loop invariants and their associated quantum Witten-Reshetikhin-Turaev theory, which is valid for all quantum invariants of links.

This study explores a novel realization of a two-dimensional chiral magnet with a distorted kagome lattice structure, focusing on a detailed theoretical analysis of its heat capacity. We utilize a mean-field approach to examine a system where the kagome lattice has been stretched along the y-axis, resulting in a semi-conductor to metal transition that can be observed as a distinct two-peak signature in the heat capacity data. This phenomenon can be reproduced using experimentally available parameters and offers a clear signature that magnetic flux per unit cell needs to surpass one for the transition to occur. Additionally, we have identified three distinct phases in the model's phase diagram based on the competition between the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic nearest neighbor exchange coupling and the next-nearest neighbor exchange coupling on the distorted kagome lattice. This study may provide a clear experimental target for the discovery of chiral magnetism in stretched kagome lattice systems.

Pre-trained language models can be fine-tuned through task-adaptation for NLP tasks, yet the generalization of this adaptation to new, unseen NLP tasks remains limited. In response, we explore the potential of task-adaptation meta-tuning, where the models learn to generalize without any prior knowledge of the new NLP task at hand. Our research reveals that task-adaptation models can indeed successfully generalize to new, previously unseen tasks, showcasing successful applications on NLI and complex NLP tasks such as knowledge-based question answering and natural language inference. Furthermore, task-adaptation meta-tuning outperforms the widely used prompt-tuning technique, and our findings suggest that task-adaptation models can learn to separate the representations of trained tasks and original, non-intentional meanings. Ultimately, task-adaptation models can be re-purposed for new, previously unseen tasks, thereby enhancing their zero-shot capabilities.

In our analysis, we investigate multiple theoretical frameworks that involve an additional $Z_2$-odd Higgs boson, namely the Inert Two-Higgs Doublet Model, several Type-II seesaw models and universal extra dimensions without chirality. These models, which, respectively, accommodate a matter anti-matter asymmetry, generate neutrino masses through fermion mixing and dark matter matter, share a common underlying structure. They all feature additional Higgs bosons that undergo the same electroweak phase transition as the Standard Model, which, absent new physics, precludes a significant deviation in the universe's baryon-to-photon ratio. A strong first-order phase transition is required for electroweak baryogenesis but is not achievable within any of these models. Our investigation conclusively demonstrates that these models are incompatible with electroweak baryogenesis under all physical constraints.

To effectively find reliable redshifts through emission lines in the millimeter/submillimeter range, we must overcome several obstacles. These include a limited number of reference sources with known positions and velocities, a scarcity of lines that accurately represent stellar motions, and the potential for multiple lines to be contaminated by dust continuum or other thermal emissions. To address these challenges, we developed an advanced method that utilizes a neural network to automatically identify multiple emission lines in observational data. This method can recognize lines of both continuum and thermal origin, is particularly suited for handling one-dimensional spectral data, and is designed to handle datasets with missing or incomplete information. Furthermore, we've adapted this algorithm to assist in cross-matching sources between datasets with differing stellar positions and velocities. Through comprehensive testing, our approach has demonstrated a high level of accuracy in producing redshifts that are in line with those from traditional methods. When applied to a sample of 100 sources with multiple thermal emission lines, our method identified the most likely correct redshift in 80% of cases. This technique is now being used to aid in the determination of reliable redshifts for the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array's ALPINA survey.

We've studied an underdoped, large anisotropy, antiferromagnetic spin system using
numerical simulations. This system exhibits a complex 120-degree ordered phase
at low temperatures, but transitions to a stripe phase at intermediate temperatures
before finally becoming a spin liquid at high temperatures. To better understand
these relationships, we analyzed the spin-only susceptibility as a function of q
vector. This study provides experimental context for recent findings related to
resonant inelastic x-ray scattering on Y$_2$BaCu$_6$O${10}$.

The study explores lattice breaking effects on the phase transition in a
lattice Higgs theory, where the temporal lattice sites, $N_t$, play a
significant role. Focusing on an $SU(3)$ Higgs theory with a fundamental
representation Higgs field, the research demonstrates that the first-order
phase transition changes to a continuous transition when $N_t=4$. The
analysis also reveals how the pseudo critical temperature, $a_T^c$, and other
observables, such as the expectation value of the Polyakov loop, the effective
mass of the temporal component of the Higgs field, and the effective masses of
the spatial components of both gauge and Higgs fields, vary with $N_t$.

This, however, is different from what density functional theory predicts. Through a combination of magnetometry, specific heat, and neutron scattering, it's found that Cr$_2$Al is a body-centered tetragonal structure with a N\'eel temperature of approximately 315 K. A new kinetic model, the $\nu$-model, was developed by Chapman and Cowling in the 1930s to bridge the gap between rarefied monatomic gas simulations and continuum fluid dynamics. It involves simplifying the complex kinetic equation by introducing an arbitrary collision frequency, leading to an intermediate single-term approximation state that includes the nu-iteration method. In this study, the nu-iteration method was initially applied to calculate properties in highly rarefied conditions. To extend its applicability to moderately rarefied situations, this study then investigated its ability to accurately predict pressure distribution around a sphere and a blunt body, as well as heat transfer around a sphere and a flat plate. Notably, this study's computed results closely matched those from the exact solution of the Boltzmann equation, as well as the direct simulation Monte Carlo method.

Voice assistants such as Alexa, Google Assistant and Siri allow users to perform a range of tasks through spoken commands.  However, their ability to execute specific online actions is restricted due to security limitations and the need for individual website authentication.  Semantic parsing has the potential to significantly improve voice assistants by enabling them to translate spoken input into actionable semantic structures, but its use currently remains limited.  This research introduces a semantic parsing framework that leverages both offline and real-time user feedback to learn from observed web interactions.  By doing so, it achieves higher parsing accuracy and more semantic representations than the available web search information alone.  Furthermore, it demonstrates how the parser can be applied to enable specific web actions in voice assistants like Alexa.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve utilizing electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions to thoroughly investigate the fundamental components of matter. To determine crucial information, precise measurements of heavy quarks formed at these high-energy interactions are essential. To gather this data, cutting-edge detectors will be required, and to analyze it, advanced flavor-sensitized reconstruction methods and jet resolution techniques will be required. We discuss the significant impact of heavy flavor hadron and jet measurements on understanding the fundamental components of matter, and the state of heavy flavor detection at present, in the context of the EIC's future. We also outline the state-of-the-art in heavy flavor detection and outline proposed solutions for both fixed-target and deep-inelastic scattering modes.

A new type of phenomenon, Quasi-Periodic Eruptions (QPEs), involves periodic gas releases near the galactic center that weren't seen before in terms of their accretion pattern. To understand their accretion process, researchers used the RASS data and compared it to X-ray observations, revealing a significant positive correlation. This suggested that the eruptions and their accretion patterns are interconnected. A simulation was conducted to explore various scenarios, and it was found that a periodic release of gas every quarter of an orbit period, caused by the supermassive black hole being perturbed by an intermediate-mass black hole, could explain both the eruptions and their accretion patterns. This could imply the existence of an intermediate-mass black hole at the galactic center.

The existence of magnetic fields in stars has long been known but its accurate measurement has been difficult due to limited understanding of how the fields behave in stars other than our own. Recent research involving new models has revealed crucial information about how the intensity of the magnetic field and the speed of the star's rotation might influence the formation of its surface features. The results indicate that the way our Sun forms surface features is closely linked to the strength of its magnetic field as it moves away from the center, and our study suggests that our Sun's magnetic field gets weaker as it moves away from the center at a rate of 10-15 kilogauss per megameter. The new models we've created seem to accurately reproduce the observed rotation speed of our Sun and predict its future changes in rotation speed.

A link exists between a Dunkl operator over a field and a conic geometry defined by an invariant form. 
In the case of the Dunkl operator with a parameter vector set to zero, the Dunkl operator reduces to a partial derivative. 
Additionally, there's a known connection between certain types of polynomials and Hermite polynomials. 
Based on prior research, we explore how a particular rank-one polynomial under a Dunkl operator relates to polynomials of a lower degree. 
Our findings reveal that for a specific type of polynomial, denoted $P_1(z) = z + \lambda$, 
a particular differential operator related to $T(z)$ is expressed as an exponential of a term involving the parameter $\alpha$. 
Specifically, we find that $\exp(\alpha)\frac{z+\beta}{\exp(\alpha)-1} - \exp(\beta)\frac{z+\alpha}{\exp(\beta)-1} = \alpha$.

Using the ATCA and the GWA21 survey, we examined 21-cm H30α emission from five nearby dwarf galaxies and analyzed their 21-cm spectral lines. Our study found that H30α is a valuable tool for accurately determining star formation rates, even in low-mass dwarf systems. We compared our findings with those of other nearby systems and discovered a relationship between the strength of H30α and the mass of the galaxies' dark matter, as well as another correlation with the strength of their 21-cm hydrogen lines. These discovered relations provide insights into the effects of low mass and gas dynamics on galaxy formation.

We demonstrate that a specific type of minimal action over an infinite compact space cannot be conjugate to two varied continuous actions with orbit equivalence, belonging to the class of Dehn's group.

We examine the approximations made in the finite-dimensional setting of the $L^2$-operator of a conditional expectation of a random variable given another. Our key finding shows that the difference between the $L^2$-operator and its best Hilbert--Schmidt approximation has a bounded operator norm that does not exceed the Hilbert--Schmidt norm itself. This outcome reveals that the $L^2$-operator can be accurately determined, essentially up to an error bound, by identifying the entries of its kernel. When dealing with the case where the under-lying probability spaces are standard, this approximation becomes even more precise, being attainable through a computationally feasible procedure.

Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models is complex due to variations in local stability and observation availability. This research provides a unified framework for constructing a family of state observers for continuous-time SEIR-type nonlinear epidemic models with non-negative states, applicable to various epidemic types. We demonstrate the existence of uniformly globally locally asymptotically stable (UGLAS) reduced-order observers with unobserved states being unobservable, provided a simple condition is met. We further examine the impact of measurement noise and contractivity of the error dynamics on observer performance through a theoretical analysis, illustrated by theoretical examples, and confirm the feasibility of UGLAS reduced-order observers through constructed Lagrange multipliers. Numerical results show that optimized state estimates from UGLAS reduced-order observers can resist measurement noise, although they may not always accurately reflect the true states. A comparative study reveals that UGLAS reduced-order observers with unobserved fluxes outperform those ignoring such fluxes in terms of both state estimation and prediction, especially for low measurement noise. We illustrate the performance of the proposed UGLAS reduced-order observers in a practical application involving COVID-19 modeling.

Many knowledge graph embedding models disregard factual temporality, resulting in
suboptimal performance for downstream tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce
Tempo, a pioneering approach for knowledge graph embedding that preserves the
temporal essence of facts. By utilizing a simple strategy to capture universal
and specific patterns, Tempo effectively represents unique historical truths,
without compromising future predictions through over-specification. Extensive
evaluations on four large-scale, real-world datasets demonstrate that Tempo
outperforms existing state-of-the-art models on both temporal and non-temporal
applications, yielding significant improvements of up to 27% for entity recommendation
and 40% for search-to-buy, while maintaining superior performance on entity link
resolution and item search tasks.

Research driven by ultrashort pulses from Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators has spawned diverse applications, with theoretical understanding rooted in conventional beam propagation analysis. However, established frameworks are often insufficient for handling the extreme demands of high-power oscillators. This study expands upon the ABCD-matrix method to examine ring resonators in high-power settings, also offering critical guidance for maintaining stable Kerr-lens mode-locking in high-power applications.

Despite its potential to protect user privacy, federated learning still encounters
several challenges, primarily due to heterogeneous client populations.
This study develops a new approach to address the heterogeneity problem, using
supervised training with contrastive learning. A contrastive loss function is
injected into each client in the central server, along with a public dataset.
Experimental evaluations demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses current
baseline comparisons, with enhanced results after just a few communication cycles.

To improve the efficiency of thin-film silicon solar cells with limited light absorption, a two-dimensional photonic band gap crystal is proposed as a replacement for the metal back reflector. Experimental results show that a V-groove array fabricated in a silicon substrate can effectively boost absorption across a broad spectrum of wavelengths, from 600 to 1000 nanometers by as much as 300 percent, while also enhancing absorption below 600 nanometers through a combination of diffraction and the surface plasmon effect. Although some decrease in absorption below 400 nanometers was observed, it can be compensated for by optimizing the anti-reflection coating.

We analyze and establish new cases of holomorphic functions requiring a key condition: 
they must behave like iterated exponentials, with a kernel that is periodic and takes on different values in the right-hand side of the complex plane. A key aspect involves understanding the asymptotic behavior of these functions as they approach the imaginary axis within the complex plane, particularly as vertical strips, where specific growth conditions must be met. Additionally, we create a framework for categorizing and asymptotically analyzing families of functions that satisfy this kernel condition, focusing on their functional dependencies. Our work also addresses a related problem: determining a function based on a given infinite-order differential equation and a prescribed set of values.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. This construction builds upon existing expander graphs and uses the randomness of uniform covers to achieve higher randomness levels. The resulting object is a simplicial complex cover that maintains higher levels of randomness despite the increase in complexity. The method leverages the relationship between random covers and the local properties of the original complex, showing that the randomness of the cover exceeds that of the graph itself. The proposed construction produces high dimensional expanders that meet strict degree constraints, achieving a product of the dimensions and a product of the dimensions less one, while also having a size that scales with n to the power of the dimension. The proof uses a combination of group theory, combinatorics, and analysis tools to verify that the constructed high dimensional expander meets all the necessary criteria.

Researchers have experimentally and theoretically investigated the magnetic and structural properties of the GdInO$_3$ single crystal. Through magnetization and muon-spin-relaxation measurements, two antiferromagnetic phase transitions at 17.5 K and 14.1 K were identified. The resulting magnetic structure is type-A, consisting of two R3h magnetic sub-lattices that are ferromagnetically aligned within themselves but antiferromagnetically aligned with the other sub-lattice. Neutron diffraction reveals magnetic moments of 7.05 and 7.08 $\mu_B$ per formula unit for the two sub-lattices, in agreement with the value of 7.08 $\mu_B$ per formula unit obtained from the magnetization data. The findings of this study are supported by first-principles calculations that utilize the spin-dependent density functional theory.

The application of graph embedding in various domains has been significant, but a major limitation exists: existing methods struggle with relevance. A key challenge is the lack of control over how well the generated node embeddings capture the underlying network structure, which is compounded by the fact that the resulting embeddings are often too densely connected, making it difficult to distinguish important information. To address these issues, a novel method called Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE) has been proposed, which takes sparse network inputs and produces a sparse, controlled-degree embedding. The proposed SSNE method is composed of two parts: a graph neural network that learns a relevant feature representation through structural characteristics, and a sparse embedding module that efficiently generates a target node's neighbors through a soft connection. A novel regularization technique based on the minimum free semidefinite program is then used to enforce a controlled degree of neighbors. The effectiveness of the proposed SSNE method has been demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on six benchmark datasets.

A low-cost water jet process is employed to achieve a 600 micron etch depth, and a 3D model predicts the achievable etch depths, as is commonly done with atomic vapor cells for low-alkali sodium and potassium atoms.

We evaluate the precision of a recently proposed nonlinear interference model for a wide range of dual-polarization 4D formats, exhibiting an average disparity with split-step Fourier simulations of no more than 0.1 dB.

Prompt wildfire detection is crucial for minimizing ecological damage, threats to human life, property damage, and transportation disruptions. To achieve this, researchers have developed various machine learning methods using different feature types, such as wavelet transform, run-length encoding, and deep learning. These techniques utilize features extracted from color, texture, and spatial domains, as well as spatial and temporal features from video streams. However, the performance of these methods heavily depends on the type of features used, as demonstrated by our proposed novel approach. This innovative technique involves using HOG-SIFT features combined with KNN classification, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods in detecting fire regions. Our proposed method surpasses the performance of recent studies by at least 1% when evaluated using the Fire109% dataset, as demonstrated through ablation studies.

Our analysis of a large Twitter dataset reveals the growth of a worldwide depression
epidemic over the past decade, with a significant increase in depression symptoms
in diverse countries. To address this, we developed a dataset for identifying
individuals with mild, moderate, or severe depression from social media texts,
enabling accurate classification. By comparing multiple machine learning models,
we found that FastText with MFDM features yielded superior performance, achieving
an accuracy of 79.77%, precision of 81.23%, recall of 78.41%, and F1 score of
80.80%. Furthermore, analyzing trends from our dataset, we observed that the
United States leads in both mild and severe depression cases, while South
Korea experiences the highest incidence of moderate depression.

This study utilizes the SIS model, a Markov chain approach, to simulate population behaviors regarding the coronavirus disease COVID-19. We create a model that accounts for external influences as time-dependent factors that impact the population's state under various COVID-19 scenarios. Our model assesses system stability and model predictability under scenarios including lockdown, quarantine, and vaccination, as well as the resumption of economic activities post-lockdown. Numerical analysis based on Bulgarian population data reveals that lifting lockdown measures accelerates the spread of the virus, whereas economic reopening reduces the number of infected individuals but does not guarantee the elimination of the disease, indicating that the infirm remain vulnerable to reinfection.

The ISGMR and $2^{+}$ isomeric states of various nuclei are investigated using a microscopic method.  A specific, $2^{+}$ isomeric state at very low energy in heavily deformed nuclei is predicted, which could serve as a direct measurement of the incompressibility modulus for these systems.  A quasi-particle hole created by removing a neutron from specific energy levels in numerically determined Gogony-Hartree-Fock-Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov ground states leads to the formation of the isomeric $2^{+}$ state.  The ISGMR $2^{+}$ excitation energy is calculated using two methods, the quasiparticle random phase approximation and a specific operator approximation, which incorporates pairing effects, in order to compare their results.  Notably, the ISGMR and $2^{+}$ IS excitation energies differ significantly, indicating a distinct separation between them.  Furthermore, studying the ISGMR excitation energies obtained reveals a clear correlation with the incompressibility modulus when using the specific operator approximation, which outperforms the quasiparticle random phase approximation in this regard.

A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of motion paths in systems governed by Coulomb friction is conducted. The existence of a universally accessible and attractive region, near a common stick-slip equilibrium, is demonstrated, regardless of initial conditions. Theoretical evidence suggests that the systems exhibit a limit cycle, featuring precisely one sliding interval, which subsequently forms the basis for the convergence path analysis. Furthermore, an upper limit on the number of sliding intervals within a convergent path is established, and a mathematical framework for estimating the upper bound of cumulative sliding durations is developed, specifically for uniform convergence regions outside the equilibrium point. The presented findings are applicable to a system consisting of two blocks on an inclined plane, interconnected by a linear spring, and the analysis is extended to systems influenced by external periodic excitation.

This paper presents a novel computational technique for effectively hedging a wide range of portfolio derivatives. The proposed model leverages a combination of financial product diversity and a new optimization strategy to address the complexity of hedging complex derivatives such as paths-dependent options. The model generates a concise set of liquid instruments such as forwards, calls, puts, and historical options, which not only provides a competitive alternative to existing portfolio hedging models but also allows for flexibility in hedging strategies when the execution of hedges becomes partially feasible due to constraints. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through two case studies involving the hedging of a portfolio of S\&P500 calls and options with path-dependent features, showcasing a significant reduction in hedging errors and the flexibility to adapt hedges when constraints are applied to specific assets.

In modern recommender systems, predicting user interactions is achieved by estimating item engagement scores, which are determined by considering the user's profile, the item's characteristics, and historical engagement data. While offline experiments effectively evaluate these systems, they often fail to account for the cumulative impact on user behavior over time, particularly the influence of users' interaction histories. To address this limitation, we developed a new framework, the Causal Tree-based Posterior (CaTaPo), to more accurately assess the performance of online-recommended systems by analyzing the causal relationships between user engagement scores and item engagement scores, taking into account the interaction histories of users. Our approach utilizes the MATE framework to simulate various offline experiments, enabling us to train, assess, and compare the efficacy of different post-training methods. The results indicate that the incorporation of post-training techniques significantly enhances the accuracy and effectiveness of online-recommended systems in predicting user engagement.

By transforming the Fuchsian equation, we derive the reduced form of the double confluent Heun equation, solving specific cases in its general form with a series when applicable. A non-geometric case with a non-integer exponent at the origin has an exact solution expressed as a convergent series for |x|<1. This non-geometric case is related to the representation of SL2(R) and SL2(C) groups. On the other hand, the exact solutions express a reducible DCHen equation for integers via a terminated series, representing the Lie group representation of a Fuchsian equation. This representation is linked to the SL2(Ap) for p a non-archimedean component of R.

Low-rank matrix recovery is an essential problem in various applications, but when different data components are affected by varying amounts of noise, standard methods often fail. We introduce a new, efficient approach, the ADMM-based weighted method, that generalizes existing techniques and enables the weighted multi-task learning problem to be solved using a single efficient algorithm with minimal changes to the code. Our approach has been successfully tested on synthetic data and real-world image projection examples, yielding significant improvements in accuracy.

In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry expectations inherent to the underlying physical laws. Our study uncovers that the vibrational modes can exhibit complex behavior, especially within regions that do not conform to the anticipated symmetry, and these are particularly pronounced at the points where different vibrational frequencies intersect. These intersections are where two or more modes become unstable and are known as exceptional points. To make this phenomenon more tangible, we derive an approximation of the ring's vibrational modes that captures their dependence on a parameter, allowing us to visualize how these points move within a diagram. This graphical representation sheds light on the intricate relationship between the vibrational modes and these critical singularities. Our findings also show that, despite being outside the realm of uniform physical conditions, these singularities can be found within a certain practical range. This discovery is corroborated by precise measurements.

We introduce the semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Universality ratio $R_\Sigma$ and investigate potential violations in our Standard Model lepton universality predictions. The rationale behind our choice of $R_\Sigma$ stems from its ability to eliminate hadronic uncertainties present in direct B-meson decay measurements. Furthermore, our analysis focuses on the partial decay width ratio of the semi-inclusive processes $B^\ast\to\rho\gamma$ and $B^\ast\to\omega\gamma$ within the framework of QCD Light-Cone Sum Rules, incorporating both leading-order contributions and next-to-leading terms, and particularly highlighting the impact of twist-3 terms that significantly affect the computed results, resulting in a difference of approximately 4 standard deviations from the predicted QCD Light-Cone Sum Rules values, and the experimental measurements by LHCb.

This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is autonomously configured based on its locally available data, leading to a decentralized design. Importantly, our approach can maintain stability even in the face of dynamic network reconfigurations, without requiring adjustments from other agents, thus ensuring seamless integration of new members and efficient controller upkeep. This robust design is enabled by leveraging Bass' algorithm to compute stabilizing controller gains through distributed solutions to Lyapunov equations.

We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique. The initial extraction utilizes a 3D convolutional neural network, and the second step employs a fully connected neural network to enhance accuracy. This approach achieved an impressive 91.67% classification accuracy on the COVIDNet-19 dataset. Furthermore, our method achieved accuracy rates of 93.33%, 100%, and 83.33% across various difficulty levels. The advanced algorithms used in our framework were implemented with the PyTorch library.

Network science is a multidisciplinary field, leveraging mathematical and computational methods to analyze complex systems through their interconnected components. Over recent decades, advancements in network science have been extensive and extensive literature on the subject is available. Despite this, a significant gap exists in comprehensively addressing fundamental concepts and historical developments in the field. This book aims to fill this void by providing an in-depth exploration of core principles, including various approaches to defining and measuring networks, essential metrics for characterizing network structures, and techniques for analyzing and reconstructing networks based on their topological characteristics. Furthermore, this book examines practical applications of network science across diverse fields such as biology, medicine, and other scientific disciplines, offering readers a comprehensive understanding of core concepts and fostering interest in further research and study.

The study of co-evolving species within their environment is an essential area of ecological and evolutionary research. Historically, this area of eco-evolutionary dynamics has focused on feedback loops and rates of evolution. However, this work considers how a global change in environmental conditions, independent of these feedback loops, affects the dynamics. A condition of global change in this work refers to an increase in temperature, which shifts the optimal phenotypic values. This work presents a comprehensive framework for analyzing eco-evolutionary dynamics under a condition of global change in environment, using a model of generalist and specialist resources interactions and temperature effects on species growth. Analysis reveals that the effects of global change in environment and rates of temperature increase on these interactions can be significantly different even for simple systems.

This research explores the potential of self-supervised learning for speech-driven text generation models, focusing on the design of upstream speech features and their impact on downstream tasks. We assess several types of key components including upstream models, downstream models, loss functions, data sets and pre-training strategies through a comprehensive experiment. Our findings indicate that a deep neural network-based generator coupled with a shallow neural network-based discriminator achieves the best results in the downstream speech synthesis task. Among various self-supervised objectives, those that emphasize frame-level local structures in speech lead to superior performance in speech synthesis and speech separation. Notably, self-supervised methods demonstrate a significant advantage over randomly initialized models by at least 60% in the weighted signal-to-distortion ratio and 20% in the weighted word error rate. Finally, we examine the effects of pre-training strategies and discover that pre-training the entire model yields the best overall performance, while pre-training just the upstream model is more effective in speech separation tasks.

Our research focuses on the underlying mechanisms of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), specifically Uniswap, and reveals a surprising finding: the instability of AMMs. AMMs are usually seen as simple and straightforward, acting like a cash machine with a fixed supply of tokens, but this assumption doesn't hold in the case of AMMs. Due to the way trades are made, the ratio of tokens changes, resulting in a loss of value for liquidity providers. This phenomenon becomes even more pronounced as traders increase their activity, highlighting the volatility of AMMs.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, has been developed to examine how inferences drawn from data with missing outcomes are affected by unverified assumptions. This technique evaluates how plausible these assumptions are by comparing estimated missing data parameters against models that don't rely on these assumptions, such as a nonparametric exchangeable likelihood model that makes no assumptions about missing data. By visualizing the relationship between model outputs and sensitivity parameters, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of how their model outputs vary based on these parameters, particularly whether the nonparamatic exchangeable likelihood assumption plausibly explains missing data. This analysis framework can be applied to any estimation task that involves missing data and relies on a complete data model. This paper showcases the utility of Sensitivity Analysis through illustrations of its application in completely missing and missing at random scenarios using complete data likelihoods, and discusses how it can be extended to missing not at random scenarios.

This study confirms the existence of additional $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries within the discrete nonlinear薛定格 equation beyond the previously discovered ones. Notably, these new symmetries involve the Cartan generator, resulting in new lattice models that are not ultralocal. Furthermore, the equation modified with these new symmetries can be viewed as a nonlinear薛定格 equation on a quantum plane. A similar approach was applied to the lattice version of the Sine-Gordon equation, also Reimann's model, however, no additional $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries were found beyond the initially known ones.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence into Internet of Vehicles applications has significant potential to generate valuable data, yet there are considerable privacy and security concerns surrounding it. A promising approach to address these issues is Federated Learning, which enables the development of confidential models without collecting sensitive data, and improves model performance by using diverse datasets. A novel solution, FL-V2X, is introduced to develop secure and efficient models within the XPIV2X simulation platform for intelligent transportation and traffic management systems. The proposed approach is tested using real-time braking distance prediction, a task requiring rapid processing and efficient use of limited resources. FL-V2X is compared against traditional approaches in different network conditions, and the results show improved performance in breaking distance prediction with better efficiency and security. Specifically, FL-V2X outperforms a global model trained on a central server by 15% in terms of root mean square error and demonstrates a 20% reduction in training time.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC has measured the production of $D_{s}^{*+}$ mesons in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV, focusing on forward regions with a rapidity between 2.2 and 4.0. The production cross sections were determined for different rapidity intervals and found to increase rapidly as rapidity increased. The resulting ratios of non-strange to strange quark production suggest that quark flavors behave like a linear distribution in rapidity. The ALICE data is compared with the results of a next-to-leading order perturbative QCD calculation and parton shower Monte Carlo simulations.

The growing importance of cryogenic cooling in quantum computing is driving the need for more capable and versatile cooling systems. Nonetheless, the high cost of extremely low-temperature cryogenics and limited supply of helium make upgrading existing systems a daunting task. To address this challenge, a novel cryogenic cooling prototype has been developed to supplement the capabilities of conventional cryogenics. This prototype prototype utilizes Gifford-McMahon cryocoolers to achieve a temperature as low as 1.5 K and will be integrated into existing dilution refrigerators to reach even lower base temperatures. A prototype platform has been designed and built to interface with 8-mm standard radio-frequency through-holes and successfully demonstrated the achievement of an ultra-low temperature of 40 mK. Future developments will focus on expanding the platform's capabilities by incorporating power distribution and signal transmission capabilities.

Previous research into Python crypto misuse has been limited to a small set of APIs, leaving a gap in understanding the broader scope of the problem. This study expands the analysis to a more comprehensive Python crypto framework, examining a vast amount of Python projects to evaluate the scope and severity of the issue. With the inclusion of submop, a new Python crypto framework that supports multiple algorithms, the study expands on the findings of a previous work by Grunwald et al. To automate the analysis, a framework was developed that integrates with the Python crypto API structure. The results from scanning 667 projects show that Python projects tend to use multiple APIs, with a subset of 20% including at least one more project using the same API, and 1% of the projects including 3 or more projects using the same API. Additionally, the study discovered that 38% of the projects, representing 257 out of 667, used at least one misuse of the tested crypto APIs, while 10 projects demonstrated crypto API reuse. Furthermore, the study found that 4 of the projects investigated in the previous work were not included in the 20% of the projects exhibiting API reuse.

This paper presents a method for 3D object localization and scene reconstruction in moving vehicles within urban environments. A framework is proposed, in which two processing units work together: one utilizes an end-to-end approach for localization, while the other reconstructs the surroundings using a neural network. Localization is carried out through an attention-based system that enhances the performance on limited data. Additionally, this proposed system aids the construction of a more reliable scene by providing a source of 3D scene information. A novel technique, combining image and depth data, has been developed to refine 3D scene reconstruction. Experiments were conducted on data collected from real-world driving scenarios and the results show that the proposed system achieves accurate 3D localization with robust performance under diverse environmental conditions and varying levels of map detail. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the system's predictions contribute positively to the construction of a more accurate scene.

We propose a novel sparse signal deconvolution approach for estimating seismic reflectivity, which relies on a statistical model of sparse signals to minimize the difference between observed and synthetic reflectivity data. To achieve this, we employ the L1 norm as a proxy for sparsity and use an iterative re-weighted L1 norm for enhanced sparse estimation. To ensure stability, we incorporate a weighted total variation norm as a regularizer in an alternating minimization framework. Our approach is evaluated using both synthetic and real data, demonstrating its effectiveness in reflectivity deconvolution through sparse signal recovery.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically examining the conditions under which these operators generate strongly continuous semigroups and their interrelation with the generator's properties. We also determine the criteria under which these semigroups can be strongly continued and present a method to calculate the generator of such semigroups.

Within the framework of bootstrap approaches, there's a central role played by the operator product expansion (OPC) coefficients in conformal field theory (CFT). These coefficients quantify how many times specific CFT operators appear when another operator is decomposed. In this work, the capabilities of the ZODIAC package for building Python-based constraint programs from CFTs are explored. Two key types of CPCs are considered: the CPC from a conformal field to a CFT operator, and the CPC from a CFT operator back to a conformal field, the latter being a novel approach. By translating CPC-based constraints into CPC-derived CPCs, the reach of CPC-based programs can be significantly expanded.

Automated part-of-speech (POS) tagging is a crucial task in linguistics,
involving assigning grammatical POS tags to words in language corpora.
While standard POS taggers operate efficiently on contemporary languages,
they often struggle with historical texts due to their unique vocabulary and
language nuances. We present a study on using deep neural networks for POS tagging
in multiple historical languages, including Old English, Old Norse, and Latin.
To address the challenge, a novel model based on bidirectional LSTM and
affix-based features has been developed. The results show that our approach
delivers consistent and accurate POS tagging results across different languages.

This research focuses on developing a method to calculate a utility function from a non-differentiable candidate of a demand function. Through an experimental approach, necessary and sufficient conditions for a valid candidate of a demand function are derived, and a method to establish continuity of the utility function is explored. An example is provided to demonstrate a case where no utility function exists, and our findings have potential applications in examining preferences for infinite commodities and related areas.

As smart cities gain momentum, they necessitate a unified method to collect, process, and exchange large amounts of data from various sources, which can be challenging to implement without a structured approach. The君 Spec project, such as CitySpec and SpecCity, seeks to utilize ontology to facilitate the creation of a standardized knowledge framework, enabling a seamless flow of data and services. This paper focuses on OASIS Process Automation Schema, an ontology-based language designed to streamline multi-organizational process design, and introduces a modified version of CitySpec tailored for smart city applications. The modified system is demonstrated through several case studies related to smart cities.

A key challenge in quantum computing is that quantum circuits are highly susceptible to errors, particularly access-related errors caused by the limited control we have over quantum bits, known as qubits. Since these errors often include inverse operations, researchers have found that incorporating these inverse operations into gates, despite being inaccessible, can help reduce them. Moreover, our study reveals that access-related errors can be modeled as modifications to quantum states, particularly changing their normalization. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that entanglement between qubits can lead to a type of error called coherence errors, caused by dephasing. Hidden inverse operations can help mitigate these coherence errors as well. Experimental results from both simulated and actual quantum devices demonstrate that using hidden inverse operations, alongside gate decompilation, can substantially lower the error rates in quantum circuits.

In a general category $\mathbb E$, taking the direct image of a partial order under a surjective epimorphism may not yield a partial order. To address this, we investigate the conditions necessary for the existence of cocartesian images of partial orders in category $\mathbb E$. These conditions are shown to naturally arise in pretoposes and categories of models of specific first-order theories, particularly in contexts related to class fields and class groups. In pretoposes, the existence of these cocartesian images can be characterized by a specific universal property involving the suprema of chains in directed graphs, a concept that has both model-theoretic and topological interpretations. Specifically, we demonstrate that cocartesian images of partial orders exist in categories with suprema of chains if and only if these suprema exist in those categories, a characterization that can be extended to pointed models of a certain type of first-order theory.

Using a multifactorial approach based on copula theory, this study investigates the joint distribution of wind speed and significant wave height in the North East Atlantic region during both day and night. Analyzing historical data collected between 1996 and 2014, the research focuses on capturing extreme events through a combination of threshold-based methods and pairwise dependence models. By comparing different spatial dependence models, such as threshold Gaussian copula and a threshold version of an elliptical copula with a shape parameter, the study demonstrates that these models accurately describe extreme events occurring in specific time periods due to their ability to model asymmetric dependence. Conversely, a threshold Gaussian copula model, although adequate for moderate events, fails to account for moderate events in case studies where the threshold is relatively low. Moreover, the findings indicate a preference for a threshold Gaussian copula in space, with the exception of specific areas along the coast where the data suggests a threshold copula with a shape parameter may be more appropriate.

Recently, large pre-trained models have achieved significant success in visual--language tasks. One notable example is CLIP, a model that learns the alignment between images and text through contrastive training on a massive dataset. However, CLIP's performance on tasks that require more complex understanding of images and text is limited by its simple loss function that just measures their alignment. We address this limitation by introducing the VIBRANT model, which is capable of representing visual attributes in a semantically-rich way. Our approach involves using a small set of text prompts to represent each image class and then applying a vocabulary embedding to these prompts to capture a broader range of attributes. We evaluate the performance of VIBRANT on five image classification tasks and demonstrate a substantial improvement over the CLIP model, particularly in few-shot settings. Our findings indicate that incorporating a semantically-aligned space for the text modality can significantly enhance representation learning tasks. The code and model of VIBRANT are available on GitHub.

To enhance computational efficiency in scientific and engineering applications, 
reducing the complexity of nonsymmetric matrix computations is essential. 
Prior methodologies for simplifying these computations have been primarily 
restricted to matrices satisfying a specific symmetry condition. 
This study expands the operator shifting framework to encompass all 
general matrices lacking inherent symmetry constraints. 
Our approach systematically transforms matrices via unitary matrix multiplication, 
prespecfying a particular set of general matrices to achieve desired computational 
goals in various scientific and engineering applications. 
For the operator-shifting process, we devise a novel method to calculate a 
family of general matrices, and demonstrate its efficacy by showing that 
extending preselected general matrix columns maintains computational 
transformation. 
Furthermore, an experimental demonstration highlights the operator-shifting 
method's capacity to enhance the solution of large-scale eigenvalue problems 
in a practical scenario.
We calculate the slices and the slice spectral sequence of integral equivariant Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra, specifically for the group $Q_8$.

Given a Noetherian local ring of positive prime characteristic with a big rational quotient, we establish that F-rationality can be determined by the non-existence of a local vanishing in a specific way, based on the characteristic polynomial of a specific endomorphism. This finding yields several consequences, including a demonstration of F-rationality in the completed local ring of a specific type of non-commutative Poisson-Voisin gerbera. Additionally, under certain conditions, we prove the Frobenius splitting stability of big-Witt rational singularities, and in the case of Gorenstein rings, we establish an equivalence between R-rationality and Frobenius purity. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between V-rationality and a specific type of homological dimension in the Grothendieck group of the ring.

The application of machine learning in clinical decision support has gained significant attention in recent years. However, a major challenge has hindered its widespread adoption - the scarcity of large, high-quality datasets for training purposes. To address this issue, researchers have developed numerous datasets for imaging analysis, but they often suffer from quality issues or are unavailable. To mitigate this concern, a robust, open-access dataset called DSC has been created, comprising a diverse collection of up to 1000 images and corresponding labels across 80 categories. Comprising nearly two million images, this comprehensive dataset spans 18511 complete scans and covers 8 primary medical fields, including CT scans, MRIs, and X-rays. DSC's primary objective is to facilitate the advancement of machine learning algorithms for medical imaging and imaging-based analysis. By supporting tasks such as medical image analysis, recognition, and understanding, this dataset is crucial for the development of reliable medical image analysis systems.

We present a derivation of Noether's current from the Einstein-Hilbert action's surface term and demonstrate that the corresponding charge is connected to Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, when evaluated on the horizon. The entropy can also be calculated using a quasi-local entropy formulation based on the horizon's causal horizon. This approach builds on the work of Brown and Hennequin for stationary black holes and extends it to include non-stationary cases. The derivation utilizes the Einstein Hilbert action's surface term and the respective Noether current for both linearized and non-linear cases. The connection between the charge and quasi-local entropy is confirmed in both scenarios, showing that it is applicable to black holes in general relativity and in various gravitational theories.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to impressive advancements in numerous biomedical applications. A significant area of research involves processing and analyzing DNA sequences in a deep learning framework, but standard deep learning models typically struggle with the variable lengths of DNA sequences. In this work, we introduce an unsupervised approach that utilizes autoencoders to learn a unified, fixed-length representation of long DNA sequences. By employing conventional autoencoders or their variants, we can identify subspace patterns within DNA sequences. A variant of the autoencoder featuring convolutional layers can also capture local features while suppressing noise. In addition, we explore a novel architecture called the graph convolutional autoencoder to learn global subspace patterns within DNA sequences. In a comparative study on multiple benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods in learning a unified representation of variable-length DNA sequences.

The interplay between a material's bulk and surface properties significantly influences its electronic behavior at the atomically thin limit. V$_2$O$_3$ films exhibit diverse metal-insulator transitions at both surface and bulk levels, driven by varying oxygen termination. In a study,  oxygen- and vanadium-terminated V$_2$O$_3$ films with four and five layers were grown using molecular beam epitaxy and analyzed using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. It was discovered that the metal-insulator transition at the surface of these films occurs at a different point than in the bulk, and is heavily influenced by surface termination. Notably, it was observed that the films' energy levels align in a way that disrupts expected metal-insulator transitions, and further analysis revealed that the surface states' dispersion patterns are unlike those of the bulk.

A new, systematic method called ALGEBRA has been created to study a class of magnetic Schrödinger systems derived from the flat dual pairs of Lie-algebroids. By using dual pairs of momentum maps, we can investigate the integrability of these systems. We have successfully applied this algorithm to a specific example: the cross-product Lie-algebroid. We have not only proven a key theorem on the complete integrability of these systems, but also discovered a set of integrating constants. Furthermore, we have constructed an efficient computational tool called ALGEBRA2, which serves as a supplemental package for the open-source computer algebra system SageMath.

The team conducted a comprehensive analysis of the exoplanet candidate MOA-1904-KUP, micro-lensed by the star HD 17133. Their model-fitting process, involving a multi-step approach, yielded a mass ratio of approximately $1.2 \times 10^{-4}$ and a planet mass of $2.2 \times 10^{-10} M_{\odot}$, corresponding to a $23 M_{\oplus}$ Earth-like body. Additionally, the result supports a semi-major axis of $1.7$ AU between the planet and its host star, and the findings also allow for an estimated distance of $6.2$ AU between the star HD 17133 and its companion, based on the measured Einstein radius, and the observed relative proper motion between the two stars.

To address a class of hyperbolic conservation law problems, a canonical example is provided through the analysis of non-linear wave equations with various boundary conditions.  The equations in question are subject to optimal control problems that accommodate multiple functionals, including those dependent on accumulated and instantaneous quantities.  The outcome of this exploration leads to characterisation results for optimal control processes.

Evaluating credit risk for bank loans is a critical task, requiring an in-depth analysis of borrowers' profiles. Traditional methods, however, have not yielded accurate predictions. This research aims to develop a reliable credit risk assessment system using contemporary machine learning techniques, leveraging non-financial applicant data. By harnessing this information, we can enhance the accuracy of risk classification. Our study involves training multiple classification models on a comprehensive dataset containing applicants' marital status, household size, employment status, employment duration, education level, and more. We compare these models using performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, and the F1-score. Our findings suggest that applying multiple machine learning models can yield better results than relying on a single approach.

Significant advancements have been made in understanding the chromatic symmetric function of specific Dyck paths and matrices with non-attacking rooks. This study builds upon these findings by exploring the chromatic symmetric polynomial of these patterns using inverse coefficients to yield novel combinatorial interpretations. We specifically examine the case of Dyck paths of length $2n$ with a descent at $n$ and derive a new combinatorial interpretation for the chromatic symmetric polynomial of these patterns, demonstrating that it shares properties with the general case of matrices with non-attacking rooks. Our analysis also reveals connections to the Catalan numbers through Eulerian polynomials, specifically showing that the chromatic symmetric polynomial of Dyck paths with a single descent at $n$ mirrors properties of the general matrix case.

This paper presents Orientation Convolution Kernels as a cutting-edge technique for generating Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs). With OCNs, regional information and its spatial orientation are effectively utilized for high-performance image recognition. Unlike traditional Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), which often struggle with training and feature representation, OCNs provide an innovative solution. By incorporating local gradient information, the proposed OCN enhances feature extraction capabilities. Furthermore, the network includes an orientation module that aligns features based on their direction, and a rotation loss is used to enhance its performance. Experimental results on the NUS-PC dataset demonstrate OCNs produce higher recognition accuracy and faster training times. Specifically, recognition rates of 81.4% are achieved within just 1000 epochs using the rotation loss, compared to 70.8% without it. Moreover, OCNs outperform the state-of-the-art (SCNN) method by 10.6% in recognition rate, largely due to its local gradient and orientation alignment capabilities. With significantly reduced parameters (1/10th) and a smaller model size (1/10th), OCNs provide a robust, high-performance solution for image recognition tasks.

Using a novel approach based on local terms of automorphic forms, we study the linearity of periodic orbits on the group $GL_{2n}$. The key innovation lies in its ability to directly yield novel level-raising theorems, which in turn determine specific characters associated with periodic orbits. By building upon the work of V. Arretche on the local trace formula, we establish the linearity of periodic orbits under certain conditions. Moreover, we extend this finding to weakly regular characters by drawing upon the discoveries made in [KLW2], and further generalize our results to include super regular characters through an analysis involving the group $Sp_{4n}$.

We develop a systematic method to study the consequences of renormalization ambiguity on the pole mass of massive quarks. This method enables us to investigate the effects on the mass of a quark when the level of precision in the perturbation theory is varied, for the cases of the charm and top quarks. We find that the rate of convergence is significantly influenced by large logarithmic expressions that arise when a quark mass is comparable to a specific energy scale. Furthermore, our analysis allows us to investigate whether variations in the perturbation series due to higher-order corrections could have a noticeable impact on parameters that are determined through perturbative calculations and experimental measurements in the cases of charm and top quarks.
