We establish a precise relationship between L^p to L^q contraction inequalities in weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk, incorporating typical weight factors and α > 1. This outcome addresses an unresolved issue in reference \cite{JANSON}, with the added consideration of cases where q is greater than or equal to 2, while providing related estimates for 0 < q < 2.

This study evaluates the diagnostic efficacy of low-dose, ultra-low-dose, and standard dose CT scans for COVID-19 diagnosis. We utilized data from 100 patients who underwent various dose levels of CT scans. We calculated the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for each dose category to assess their diagnostic performance. Additionally, we developed a virtual dose reduction technique to convert standard dose images into lower dose equivalents. Our results indicate that low-dose and ultra-low-dose CT scans achieve similar diagnostic accuracy to standard dose scans. We also found that the proposed virtual dose reduction method generates images comparable to those obtained from experiments.

As numerous satellite constellations are being planned in low-Earth orbit,
effective management of the limited space available is crucial. Although
occupying the same orbital shell, satellites do not necessarily interact with one
another. By analyzing space occupancy, which measures the probability of a random
point within the shell being inside a sphere, we can gain insight into the vast
empty spaces surrounding Earth. Our findings reveal that although a significant
number of satellites are in operation, their collective mass has minimal impact
on Earth's atmosphere. Moreover, we observe a gradual increase in debris
causing a buildup in the lower region of the shell. By examining the altitude
distribution of objects, we examine the idea of a "graveyard" orbit and highlight
the importance of further research and development to preserve orbital stability.

To generate high-quality quadrilateral meshes, an innovative method is introduced that utilizes boundary curves in three-dimensional space to facilitate automated meshing of two-dimensional regions. This framework is built on top of the SPASM meshing algorithm, which supports the creation of high-order quadrilateral meshes using high-quality quads and potentially other polygon types. A new incremental polygon removal approach is developed to improve flexibility and efficiency, reducing the complexity of initial triangular meshes. This reduction in mesh complexity enhances performance and further boosts mesh quality. Additionally, the framework demonstrates its versatility and robustness through its application to various difficult three-dimensional surfaces, including the creation of high-order quadrilateral meshes on the outer skin of the Boeing 787 Dreamliner.

Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently employed as a measure of association in statistical analysis. The strength of evidence for linear correlation is often evaluated using a hypothesis test, such as the t-test, which is understood to be equivalent to the likelihood ratio test under normality. The aim of this work is to derive accurate, compact, and easily interpretable confidence intervals for correlation under both marginal and bivariate normal distributions. The proposed methods for confining correlation rely on the roto-translational invariance of correlation and the existence of monotone transformations that convert any distribution into a standard normal distribution. The validity of the new confidence intervals relies on the delta method, the continuous mapping theorem, and the fact that any distribution can be transformed into a standard normal distribution. The methods' performance is evaluated through simulations, while a case study demonstrates their application in practice.

We create a framework for two-body scattering in classical gravity.  We utilize information from a previous study of the same scattering problem within QFT in curved spacetime.  This framework lays the groundwork for a future application of the EFT method.  We also show that our approach is equivalent to a previous two-body calculation published in 2021 by B. P.  We further adapt our method to address two-body calculations involving heavier particles, building on calculations related to QFT in curved spacetime.  To simplify the application of our approach, we provide a code for two-body scattering when the speed is slower than the gravitational field.  We show that our approach accurately reproduces results from a previous calculation related to QFT in curved spacetime and baryon and lepton dynamics, as well as those of B. P. and B. A., and that we can use our approach to predict outcomes that have not yet been calculated.

We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined within a bounded region. Our findings show that initial conditions,, in the $L^3(\mathbb{R}^3)$ space exhibit small data well-posedness within a Cauchy problem of the Navier-Stokes equations. Furthermore, this stability of the solution is preserved in the case where the boundary is sticky. The method involves establishing an inequality for the $L^2-BMO^{-1}$ norm of the velocity field, which is valid for all time. The approach also enables one to obtain a precise estimate of the boundary layer, and, hence, adapt the two-dimensional method of Escauriaza, Seregin and Sverak to fit the three-dimensional situation.

Language learning dictionaries can aid students in deciphering unknown words within texts by supplying word definitions. However, conventional dictionaries often fail to consider the contextual connections between words. A novel, interactive dictionary called ContextLearn was designed to learn a word's context from the texts students study and make that knowledge available in a dictionary-like interface. Our study examined ContextLearn's effect on 112 students' vocabulary acquisition, showing that it enhanced acquisition of words not explicitly defined. Furthermore, our results indicated that students' acquired vocabulary correlated positively with class-level word frequency distribution. A follow-up study involving 22 teachers revealed ContextLnear was engaging and suitable for secondary students, though some teachers noted it might be less effective for very abstract words.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to a surge in research on explainable recommendation systems. Despite existing solutions, the focus has primarily been on improving system performance rather than exploring key aspects of user experience, such as trustworthiness and clarity, within the context of recommenders. This paper addresses this gap by exploring the challenge of creating explainable recommendation systems that are both transparent to users and enhance trust in the system. To this end, I've introduced a new framework, XR, which assesses the user experience in a range of feature counterfactual explanation methods for recommenders. The experimental findings reveal significant variations among different methods, with those that reveal the characteristics of unchosen items often result in user distrust. In contrast, those that provide explanations based on recommendations or make recommendations consistent with user preferences generally enhance the user's trust. The study also suggests that user experience research should involve not only open-ended surveys but also more controlled, automated approaches to gather feedback.

Quantum wells made of InAs on a InP substrate are an ideal candidate for high-speed, short-wavelength optoelectronic applications.  The'shallow' energy band structure of InAs allows the creation of quantum wells with a very thin confinement region, but this comes with the added challenge of maintaining a smooth surface to ensure high electron mobility.  To address this, the growth of high-quality MQWs using molecular beam epitaxy has been thoroughly investigated.  The growth conditions, the structural and morphological properties, and the electrical characteristics of the MQWs were analyzed using various techniques.  The results indicate that the smoothness of the surface is the most critical factor influencing electron mobility.  The optimal surface current density of the growth is $2\times10^9$ atoms $cm^{-2}s^{-1}$, and the resulting MQWs exhibit the highest electron mobility of approximately 80,000 $cm^2 V^{-1} s^{-1}$, along with a distinct first and second conduction band at 15 and 34 meV, respectively, and a distinct 53 meV inflection point in the binding energy spectrum of the MQWs.  The inflection point of the well matches the theoretical inflection energy of the well.

This study introduces an unsupervised robust learning framework that leverages self-supervision and queries to detect anomalies, allowing it to adapt to various unsupervised scenarios, both supervised and unsupervised. The proposed robust learner, denoted as $\mathcal{R}$, is designed to extract a reliable model representation, $\mathcal{M}$, from clean training data, and is able to perform local membership queries (LMQs) to ask the model for predictions, thereby enhancing its adaptability and performance. The robust learner, $\mathcal{R}$, consists of two essential components: a self-supervised loss function, $\mathcal{L}_{self}$, which measures the discrepancy between predicted and actual data distributions, and a loss function, $\mathcal{L}_{model}$, which adjusts the model based on the results of the self-supervised queries. The proposed self-supervised loss function, $\mathcal{L}_{self}$, is task-agnostic and adapts to different data scenarios without requiring adjustments. The experimental findings indicate that the proposed robust learner, $\mathcal{R}$, exhibits exceptional performance on anomaly detection tasks and generalizes well to clean data.

Our previous research demonstrated the existence of novel mathematical matrices called the Low Rank Uncertain Coherent Tensor (L/U-CoLT) that meet specific criteria. This study delves into the properties of L/U-CoLT, highlighting how basic mathematical matrix operations can be executed with efficiency. Furthermore, a specific type of LTHT matrix, Subspace L/U-CoLT (Sub-L/U-CoLT), is defined, and a quantum algorithm is developed to accomplish matrix-vector multiplication involving Sub-L/U-CoLT in linear time. This algorithm is efficient, with both its forward and backward iterations being latching-free and thus operating within linear time. A thorough analysis of the Sub-L/U-CoLT matrix is conducted, focusing on its properties and relationships with quantum state tomography, where it is shown that any quantum state can be represented using a combination of Sub-L/U-CoLT matrices. This discovery allows for an optimized quantum algorithm for state tomography, where the number of measurements required decreases with the square root of the dimension of the matrix's support. This study contributes to the fields of quantum computing, low-rank tensor mathematics, and tensor network states, with applications in machine learning, tensor networks, and low-rank matrix completion.

Young stars emit intense high energy radiation, potentially altering nearby planets' atmospheres and influencing habitability. Observations of young stars in the near-infrared spectrum allow us to study their high energy radiation, though direct measurements are rare due to limited sensitivity. We studied the young solar analog K2-33, a star in the Taurus molecular cloud, using a spectrograph, but found it lacked sufficient sensitivity for an accurate measurement. Consequently, we employed a machine learning model to estimate X-ray and UV emission based on near-infrared spectral data. We compared our results with those of other young stars and found X-ray and UV flux values consistent with previous measurements, providing a new approach to studying young stellar emission in a sample of ten stars from the Taurus molecular cloud.

We investigate an extended version of the Bethe-Hocheist formula, accounting for the effects of mechanical friction within the medium and interactions between the charged particle and the medium's phonons. Our analysis reveals that mechanical friction and coherent phonon production lead to the same energy loss mechanism, but the incoherent phonons created due to the breaking of spherical symmetry in the energy-momentum space reduce the energy lost to the medium by a factor, dependent on the momentum.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, the majority class often overwhelms the training process, leading to subpar performance. One effective solution to mitigate this issue involves a reweighing technique that assigns class-specific weights to training samples, thereby adjusting the influence of the majority class. This research builds upon the Least Squares Classifier (LSC) by incorporating reweighing methods, including the LSC-OWA and LSC-OWA2 approaches. LSC-OWA utilizes an ordered weighted average function to assign dynamic class-specific weights based on the respective class sizes. Conversely, the LSC-OWA2 technique assigns static class-specific weights and then applies a reweighing mechanism during the training phase. Both models demonstrate a classification error rate comparable to that of the AdaBoosting algorithm, with LSC-OWA2 showing significantly improved execution times.

We present our novel artificial neural network-based pipeline for identifying extremely distant (high-redshift) quasars from spectroscopic data. This system employs a boosting algorithm to enhance feature selection and optimizes a single-layer perceptron to achieve better classification accuracy. Our pipeline's performance is then tested on simulated spectra from redshift 3 to 6 and compared to established classification methods, such as random forests and neural networks. Our pipeline is subsequently applied to the spectrum of a recently discovered quasar candidate, IZT180218A, at a redshift of approximately 6.1. Utilizing the pipeline, we calculate the classification probability of the IZT18018A spectrum and determine it to be a quasar with high confidence. Furthermore, we use the quasar's emission lines to constrain its physical properties and calculate a rest-frame V-band magnitude of approximately 20.3, making it one of the most luminous known quasars at such a high redshift. Finally, we fit the QSO luminosity function derived from the Pan-STARRS QSO candidate catalog, and obtain slope values of -1.02 and -0.71 for the luminosity function at redshifts between 3<z<4.5 and z>6, respectively.

We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to directly monitor the phase-coherent tunneling of charges, a process that occurs within the Measleya effect and can be accessed through the quantum dot's response at an energy-splitting level. This was done with a quantum dot carefully isolated from its superconducting neighbor, ensuring that the interaction was weak and allowed for the fine-tuning of a resonance. This was possible due to the quantum dot's ability to act as a tunable impedance sensor and was further confirmed with a model that explains the observed data. This discovery sheds new light on the properties of the quantum dot-superconductor system and could potentially lead to significant advancements in related fields of research.

Our work establishes the conditions under which certain types of shocks in systems of conservation laws will propagate and remain stable over time. Specifically, we focus on the behavior of weak solutions for a specific model representing compressible, viscous fluids. In this context, the measure of stability is determined by the continuity of the fluid's energy and its rate of change.

We explore both the strengths and weaknesses of conditional image generation based on recent gains in regional extrapolation using Conditional Diffusion Models. This field has shown significant potential in regional extrapolation, surpassing previous gains based on GANs. This is largely due to its ability to make subtle style adjustments and accurately capture complex distributions. This conditional generation framework has been widely applied in a variety of tasks, from artistic creations to filling gaps and completing images. This study examines how Conditional Diffusion Models perform in regional extrapolation tasks and compares their performance to established conditional GANs. We explore different conditional strategies, analyze the current limitations, and suggest areas for future research.

Many complex systems are modeled using network theory, where nodes and connections represent relationships between entities like social connections or brain neurons. These networks often exhibit stochastic behaviors due to external influences, leading to diverse and dynamic outcomes. To study such behaviors, researchers have developed various analytical tools, including time-series analysis and spectral analysis. This review explores methods for analyzing large-scale networks with random dynamics, emphasizing techniques that can identify significant patterns within noisy data.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This research focuses on a method to assess liquid-solid slip in terms of its effect on a specific condition known as the Bond number for surface tension. We consider a liquid film on a fiber with a specific pattern of density stratification that causes the film to be unstable and begin to break into drops. Our findings indicate that allowing liquid slip on the fiber increases the rate of these breaks, which in turn affects the distance between the drops. This, in turn, enables us to calculate a suitable Bond number that can be used to compare different types of fluids in terms of how they stick to the surface they're flowing over. This comparison is essential for studying the dynamics of complex fluids in terms of how they behave when flowing over different surfaces.

We investigate how sensitive unique $\alpha$-dissipative solutions are to small changes in their starting points in the context of the Carnot-horizontal systems of differential equations. We establish that for any given time frame, the solutions adhere to a specific mathematical limit as the starting points become arbitrarily close, indicating that the solutions are Lipschitz stable. We leverage the findings to identify optimal rates at which the density of $\alpha$-dissipative solutions converges when approximated by a Carnot-horizontal flow in the scenario where $\alpha$ equals $\tfrac12$.

Measuring the curvature of scoliosis is crucial, but a key aspect is the reliability and efficiency of measurement tools. While manual or automated methods have been used, they often have limitations in terms of precision and speed. This study proposes a novel approach to assessing scoliosis curvature by utilizing robotic ultrasound scanning. This method involves analyzing images acquired by a robotic probe, which can be precisely controlled along a curved spine. By controlling the probe's angle, this system ensures a consistent measurement of the curvature, leading to a reliable and user-independent result. This approach was successfully applied to a simulated scoliosis with known curvature, demonstrating a high level of accuracy in the measured curvature. Furthermore, this method can also be used to automatically locate the peak of the curvature, which is essential for proper clinical evaluation. Overall, this robotic approach offers a promising solution for accurately and reliably measuring scoliosis curvature.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modeling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a RNN model to predict distribution values and utilizing a pre-trained TiMi-D model to guide the training process. Like TiMi-D, this model predicts quantiles for given phoneme context and forcing variables, but it innovatively predicts a set of quantiles that represent different distributions. A novel feature of this model is its ability to utilize a distribution, such as GT-MMSE or a Gaussian model, to guide the training and determine the required quantiles. During inference, a selection mechanism is employed to choose the most suitable predicted quantile for each phoneme based on the predicted distribution values. This model was tested on the Ais3 dataset and demonstrated a mean absolute percentage error of 9.42%, which outperforms the PEASS-2019 best model's 10.04%, but it was found to be less effective than the PEASS-2020 best model's 7.94%. Moreover, this model shows improved performance over its predecessor in terms of adaptability. Finally, the model's performance was evaluated through a listening test, revealing a preference for its method over the PEASS-2020 best model, particularly in terms of handling variation.

Identifying online hate speech has become a significant concern for researchers due to its impact on digital safety. Studies have revealed the prevalence of offensively language that is sexist, racist, and sexually offensive. While the severity of this language is evident, the impact on social media platforms is not as pronounced as one might expect. We conducted an experiment, which involved showing participants a series of profiles on Facebook and Twitter alongside hate speech content. We examined how they responded to these posts in terms of sharing, liking, and commenting on them. Our research involved over 1,000 participants, who were exposed to 150 posts on Facebook and 150 posts on Twitter. We also analyzed how participants reacted to the content based on their own ethnic and gender identities. The results showed that people tend to disengage from and avoid sharing, liking, or commenting on online hate speech. We provide an in-depth analysis of the underlying motivations for this behavior and discuss the implications of our findings.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks incorporate all possible cross-term interactions between inputs in regression tasks, enabling a comprehensive feature engineering process without human intervention. However, using MIMO networks in their standard form is not efficient with parameters and causes overfitting due to training each model independently. Ensembling improves performance but comes at the cost of even greater parameter wastage. To resolve overfitting and save parameters, our research introduces a new technique that merges two different approaches - entangled induction variable dropout (EIVD) and a new optimization method. Enabling dropout input variable inference in traditional neural networks has previously been possible but led to waste and overfitting. Enabling induction variable dropout in MIMO networks had not been explored before. To prevent overfitting, our research introduces a method to match input variable entanglement, ensuring consistent performance even when some variables are dropped out during training. To save parameters, our research introduces a technique to induce shared weights between individual cross-terms, significantly improving efficiency and performance on multiple datasets in comparison to competing methods.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing datasets employed in document image analysis research. Document image analysis examine the contents of document images and are a/an key challenge to multiply tasks. For a better understanding of existing research, we have conducted a thorough examination of numerous datasets, categorizing them by their inherent difficulties, and provided an evaluation of their respective search strategies. In addition, we have utilized modern knowledge graph research to create a readily accessible website featuring information on these datasets. Ultimately, we have pinpointed potential future research directions.

In manufacturing, a critical issue arises from robot structural changes, primarily caused by wear, dynamic movements, and workpiece loading. To accurately control and manage these transformations, researchers are focusing on developing a method to precisely measure and represent these changes, referred to as robot intrinsic flexibility. In this study, we present W2O-Flex, an approach to model and analyze the structural deformation of industrial robots, accounting for the effects of workpiece mounting and manipulation. In contrast to previous methods primarily studying the changes along the robot's axis, W2O-Flex examines structural changes across all axis using an in-depth, non-contact measurement technique and data analysis. By modeling the deformation as a function of the workpiece and end-effector configurations and mapping the changes at key points on the robot body, we provide an effective method to monitor and reduce these structural changes through online optimization techniques to improve positioning accuracy and task performance.

The health outcomes of individuals are heavily influenced by their early life experiences. Understanding these trajectories is essential for developing effective public health interventions, particularly for those with a genetic predisposition to certain conditions. We have developed a new growth model, the Ancestral Polynomial Regression Model (APRM), that not only fits individual growth patterns but also identifies a common growth trajectory. This model combines the statistical methods of spline functions and clustering to achieve a balance between a diverse common trajectory and well-fitted individual growth patterns. We evaluated APRAm through simulation studies and found it outperformed alternative models in predicting growth patterns. We have successfully applied this model to data from the ALSPAC study to investigate the growth patterns of boys at different ages. The results revealed varying growth patterns among boys with and without a genetic predisposition to certain conditions at ages 5, 9, and 11 years old.

One widely-used approach to calculating electronic integrals for complex molecules is the Becke's partitioning scheme. To enhance this method, a novel algorithm has been developed to efficiently identify the nearest atoms for each point within a grid, crucial to calculating electronic integrals in polyatomic molecules. To minimize computational costs, the algorithm combines techniques including a grid reduction method and multiple levels of screening to reduce complexity. Additionally, the algorithm has been optimized to utilize multi-threading and distributed computing capabilities. Its performance was tested and validated using a range of molecules, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness and compatibility with other methods when combined with a distributed computing framework.

In a graph G, a subset R of its vertices forms a resolving set when, for any two distinct vertices g1 and g2 in G, there's a vertex r in R that's closer to g1 than to g2 in terms of distance. The resolving set with the minimum number of vertices in this group is known as the metric dimension of G, denoted by \beta(G). A strong edge labeling or a SE-labeling, is a specific type of edge labeling on a graph, where each vertex's incident edges can be uniquely identified based on the labels of those edges. The smallest number of vertices needed to be marked with these special labels is known as the strong edge labeling number of G, denoted by \seil(G). The main goal of this paper is to explore the relationship between \seil(G) and \beta(G) in graphs with a specific structure or in specific graph families.

Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to the context of continuous functions on domains of computation.  It explores their properties, particularly the monad structure, and examines how they compare to their continuous functions, providing a useful tool for the semantically rich description of non-deterministic programming languages.

Evaluating how thorny devil lizards' water absorption ties into atmospheric circulation is an important issue. To address this, we use statistical models to analyze data from Australian hothouse climates and examine its connection to global climate patterns. This study reveals that in areas where the water cycle is intense, like those with hot and dry climates, the atmospheric circulation tends to fluctuate more than it does in other time periods. By investigating how these fluctuations behave, we find that simple explanations do not suffice. Instead, we turn to a more complex model that takes into account multiple time scales and competing processes. This approach is more effective in accurately describing the water absorption patterns of thorny devils, and its success may hint at a more widespread role for atmospheric circulation models in understanding how these creatures obtain and manage water, particularly in hot and dry environments.

The application of deep learning in medical imaging has shown promising outcomes, but the process of labeling large datasets of medical images proves to be both time-consuming and costly. Consequently, a significant amount of noise is often introduced during the labeling process, leading to models that struggle to generalize and perform poorly when faced with real-world scenarios. To tackle this issue, researchers propose a novel approach, which involves using weakly-supervised learning to enable models to learn from limited labels, while simultaneously addressing the challenges posed by noisy labels and uncertain class labels. The proposed approach demonstrates substantial improvements in robustness, outperforming existing methods, as evidenced by its performance in experiments involving breast ultrasound images, where data was intentionally corrupted to simulate real-world conditions.

The support of $\hat{f}$ lies within the dual group $\hat{G}$ and can be a discrete set. In the study, the authors investigate the compact set $Q_n$, and define a norm $\|\cdot\|_0$ for the space $C(Q_n)$. The central problem they aim to solve involves constructing an interpolation operator $P$ on $C(Q_n)$, such that $P$ preserves the space of Chebyshev polynomials of degree at most $n$, and for all $h \in C(Q_n)$, the norm $\|Ph\|_0$ does not exceed a certain constant times $\|h\|_0$, with the constant being independent of $h$. The proposed interpolation operator $P$ corresponds to interpolation at the zeros of a specific polynomial $P_n(x)$, and the study aims to establish an upper bound, which is independent of $n$, for the associated Lebesgue constant, given the function $P_n(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \hat{p}_j \bar{E}_j(x)$, where $\hat{p}_j$ are the non-zero discrete Fourier coefficients of $pf$. A correlated random walk (CRW) is derived from the Grover matrix, the evolution matrix of the Grover walk on a graph. It is defined by a parameter $\rho\in[-1,1)$, representing the average degree of the graph, except for regular graphs where it aligns with the degree. By expressing the CRF's transition matrix $P$ as the ratio of two polynomials in $\rho$, we can establish an identity involving the coefficients of a polynomial $f$ and the $k$-th distance zeta function $\Delta_k(s)$ of the graph. This relationship allows us to derive a decomposition of the CRW into sums of power laws with zeta-modulated terms and to analyze the asymptotic behavior of $P^n$ as $n$ tends to infinity using the roots of the polynomial $f$.

In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations.

The accuracy of a widely used empirical formula for predicting skin-friction drag in wall-bounded flows has been systematically assessed. The formula in question was first validated through comparisons with direct numerical simulation data for various geophysical and engineering flows, including channel, pipe and turbulent boundary layer scenarios. These comparisons revealed that the empirical relation effectively models the primary drive for the growth of skin-friction drag with respect to Reynolds number, however it is lacking in fully accounting for secondary effects related to geometry and G$\pi$. A more thorough analysis was then conducted using high-resolution data recovery from direct simulation results for a comprehensive collection of wall-bounded flow scenarios, thereby providing new insights into the secondary effects on skin-friction drag. These results led to a reassessment of the accuracy of the empirical relation and a reassessment of its limitations, including a quantification of the errors involved and an analysis of how these errors vary with secondary effects. This reevaluation ultimately resulted in a more accurate model for predicting skin-friction drag, which significantly reduced errors across a diverse set of wall-bounded flow scenarios.Humanity's long-term memory is a vast and intricate knowledge system that has evolved over centuries, encompassing diverse scientific, cultural, and societal aspects. Over the past decade, the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has led to a surge in the development of sophisticated models for language understanding and generation. This study examines the properties of self-dual solitons within a five-dimensional, real scalar field theory that exhibits a non-local potential. In the limit of small soliton mass, we derive a non-symmetric non-linear differential equation for the soliton profile, and compare it with a corresponding equation from a local field theory that supports a self-dual soliton of the same type. Furthermore, we use numerical methods to analyze soliton solutions in both the non-local and local cases, and explore how their shapes and masses differ. Notably, our results reveal that the soliton solution in the non-local case is characterized by a more pronounced, asymmetric tail compared to its local field theory counterpart.

For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model in a magnetic field, where the effect of orbital magnetism is broken, we investigate the behavior of Weyl nodes in a 202-site dimer chain with a magnetic field applied. The research identifies configurations of Weyl nodes under different conditions of magnetic field and model parameters. By adjusting a model parameter, we can control the type of Weyl node configuration, such as pairs, quadruples, or nodes of different orientations. The study also examines the relationship between the orientation of Weyl nodes and the magnetic field, as well as the behavior of orbital magnetism in relation to the magnetic field, revealing a potential for local magnetism but not global magnetism due to orbital effects.

This research paper presents a strategy to develop high-performance optical devices that meet specific optical requirements. The absorption of light from an emitter within a patterned structure is enhanced through a mechanism known as Purcell effect, which in turn enables directed emission of light. The design of these devices is based on a simple, thin, and flexible substrate made of plastic, incorporating a reflective layer and a reflective coating. The emitter is embedded within this structure, allowing for efficient and flexible optical applications.

Mechanical screening, a widely observed effect where increasing pressure leads to changes in one property without significantly affecting others, has been extensively studied primarily in the context of uniform, external influences. Conversely, we have developed a novel approach examining the concept of intrinsic screening, driven by internal stresses within the material itself. To do this, we've analyzed the behavior of amorphous solids composed of interconnected oscillators under specified, external pressures, resulting in internal stresses. We've identified two contrasting regimes - one characterized by 'weak screening', where internal stresses don't substantially modify the material's response to external pressure, and another marked by 'strong screening', where internal stresses can significantly alter or even eliminate the material's response to external pressure. Moreover, we've established a framework to predict whether a material will exhibit 'weak' or 'strong screening', based on inherent properties.

Silicene's unique Dirac fermion properties have been hindered by its interaction with metallic substrates, but here we explore how to overcome this limitation by growing it on a hexagonal boron nitride layer. Utilizing density functional theory, our simulations reveal a significant opening of the band gap, reaching approximately 100 meV at the $\Gamma$ point in the band structure. Moreover, by manipulating the number of electrons within the unit cell through doping or gating, we've discovered a pathway to control the band gap size, showcasing potential for innovative applications. These findings have important implications for various novel electronic technologies and materials, including topological insulators, superconductors, and semimetals.

Recent observations from the Event Horizon Telescope have revealed that material falling into the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way is ejected as a supernova remnant known as Sgr A East. This remarkable discovery has sparked interest in understanding the origin of this enigmatic remnant. We conducted a thorough analysis of the relic's properties, drawing from a comprehensive set of multi-wavelength observations. Our investigation focused on the spectral energy distribution of the relic, which spans from radio to gamma-ray wavelengths. We found that the relic's energy release peaked around the soft X-ray band and that its radio emission exhibited a distinct synchrotron profile. This led us to develop a time-dependent model of the relic's synchrotron emission and to estimate its age at approximately 16-19 years. We also analyzed the Fermi-LAT data on high-energy photon emission from the relic and found that it could be produced by the inverse Compton scattering of various low-energy photon fields off electron populations accelerated in shock waves or at particle injectors. Our study indicates that the Sgr A East relic was likely created during a gamma-ray burst event in 1973-1974, most probably a gamma-ray burst resulting from a neutron star merger.

The study examines various data augmentation techniques, such as SMOTE, to tackle class imbalance classification issues. It reveals that traditional approaches, combining resampling and classification methods, have limitations. In contrast, a novel two-stage algorithm integrating nearest neighbor and gradient boosting algorithms is proposed to classify imbalanced data. Unlike existing methods that overfit reduced samples or oversample, this approach avoids such problems. It was tested on multiple datasets and demonstrated superior performance, outdoing other methods like Random Forest and k-NN.

During the COVID-19 outbreak, an examination of viral social media posts related to the national health crisis revealed information, opinions, and rumors. By analyzing these events and their timing in early 2020, researchers discovered that viral Twitter posts about COVID-19 were initially closely correlated with news reported in major national outlets but were ultimately inversely related, before falling apart. Conversely, when it came to local news and Twitter feeds within the same geographic areas, both in large and small cities, both in English and Spanish, they all showed a consistent and inverse correlation with each other throughout the entire COVID-19 timeline. Furthermore, based on a model of an information epidemic, it was discovered that there was a widespread belief among online COVID-19 posts that the virus originated in China. Lastly, by analyzing the linguistic style of online COVID-19 posts, researchers discovered that online conspiracy-laden content was more likely to originate from a smaller number of sources. These findings suggest that an investigation of spatiotemporal patterns combined with an analysis of viral social media content can offer valuable insights into public health crises.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses inherent conservation attributes when properly formulated. The present research proposes a novel, locally consistent, and unconditionally stable scheme for enforcing entropy while maintaining a universal advection framework. By employing a universally consistent advection scheme, mass, momentum, and total energy are conserved, while entropy is non-decreasing. We demonstrate that this scheme preserves galactic and Jensen's inequalities through a finite entropy production term derived from the thermodynamic relationship. The results of the theoretical framework are corroborated by two-dimensional simulations comparing the performance of various schemes.

Numerical studies investigating the $Q^2$ dependence of the ratio $G_E/G_M$ in elastic electron-proton scattering have been conducted to examine how varying $G_E/G_M$ impacts longitudinal polarization transfer in reactions involving real photons and protons. These simulations explore two reactions: real-photon proton scattering and deep-inelastic scattering with neutrons. It's found that an increasing $G_E/G_M$ ratio with increasing photon energy results in enhanced polarization transfer, conversely, that with further increasing $s$, polarization transfer intensifies due to the enhanced $G_M$ cross section, resulting in its higher transverse helicity components. Ultimately, results suggest that measurements of the recoil-proton polarization can offer insight into the $G_E/G_M$ ratio.

We introduce a novel approach to leverage artificial states for enhancing both reinforcement and imitation learning methods in a data-efficient manner. Our proposed method involves generating hypothetical states to incorporate them into the learning process, coupled with a weighted average of real and synthetic states. Incorporating synthetic states allows the system to mitigate the biases introduced by the limited and potentially unbalanced distribution of state observations during training. In reinforcement learning, this leads to a more balanced data distribution for state transitions, while also reducing the impact of off-policy corrections. For imitation learning, we demonstrate that incorporating synthetic states helps counter the bias caused by the limited state distribution in the training data. Our extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of our approach, showcasing, for example, a 2.4 times improvement in data efficiency over the current state-of-the-art DDPG algorithm on the Half-Cheetah v2 environment for task generalization in reinforcement learning.

A comprehensive search for the simultaneous production of two Higgs bosons is being carried out, utilizing data with a total luminosity of 137/fb collected by the ATLAS detector using 13 TeV protons. This study focuses on a final state characterized by one b-tagged Higgs boson decaying into a pair of b-quarks and the other Higgs boson decaying into a pair of photons. Simulations were performed under the assumption of an additional non-resonant production mechanism typical of a broad Higgs boson predicted by theories beyond the Standard Model. Under these theories, and at 95% confidence levels, a limit of 3.1 times the Standard Model prediction was established as an upper bound on the simultaneous production of Higgs bosons.

Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillation are capable of achieving high sensitivity and extensive dynamic range in measurements. Modern technologies allow for the miniaturization of these magnetometers and the integration of them into portable devices. In this study, a magnetic field sensor was developed that utilizes an integrated semiconductor spiral inductor, which was coupled with a self-oscillating atomic magnetometer situated in a localized magnetic field. Using the zero-crossing detection method, the frequency shift in the magnetometer's oscillation was measured and calculated to determine the magnetic field's strength. This method demonstrated a correlation between the frequency shift and the magnetic field's strength, as well as demonstrated the method's potential for real-time monitoring of magnetic field variations associated with biological activity in human brains and dental implants. This method represents a novel concept that combines atomic magnetometry with modern microfabrication techniques to create a magnetic field sensor adaptable for various applications.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the analysis & synthesis method allows us to construct such K3 surfaces, K3 logarithmic schemes, or K3 surface logs, as desired, by choosing any even integer from $0$ to $18$ for the rank or the Sato-Tate log-Siegel surface type.

A supergravity unified framework is examined with the aim of determining the neutralino's role as a suitable dark matter candidate. This involves solving a system of nonlinear equations to calculate crucial parameters for the model. A detailed exploration is conducted around the parameter space, specifically around the dark matter neutralino mass threshold. This assessment evaluates the model's compatibility with current dark matter search experiments and thorough analyses are carried out regarding the dark matter neutralino's production in proton-proton collisions and its detection via direct and indirect methods.

The Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme (EPTAS) has been established for finding the maximum independent set in bipartite graphs with large minimum degree. We enhance this achievement substantially by reducing the approximation error to a function solely dependent on the parameter k for bipartite graphs exhibiting large minimum degree. We then investigate the possibility of a similar EPTAS on general graphs with a similar property. We introduce a new algorithm achieving an O(k log k) approximation, relying on both a known Hitting Set EPTAS and the conjecture that General SAT can be solved quasilinearly in a parameter-dependent manner. We further explore potential generalizations of our results, including an algorithm providing an F(k) approximation in time T(n) with F(k) being subexponential in k and F(k) being sublinear in k for bipartite graphs in time T(n).

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly reducing required communication rounds compared to existing distributed algorithms. Convergence analysis and performance evaluation through simulations demonstrate the algorithm's performance, highlighting a 10-fold improvement over current approaches.

Our approach to training a neural network for detecting hate speech in Hindi and Bengali involves leveraging a scarce annotated dataset by combining multiple techniques. First, we increase the training data through multiple augmentations, such as word replacements using synonym replacement and back translation. Additionally, we replace nouns and adjectives with randomly selected relevant terms to preserve the original text's meaning. We also train the model using multiple pretrained language models, specifically Simple Hindi Model and Burmese Language Model. Finally, our ensemble model, which integrates multiple neural network architectures, achieves a macro-F1 score of 81.46% on the Hindi dataset and 79.68% on the Bengali dataset in a microaveraged F1 measure.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to distinguish the direction of nuclear recoils is highly beneficial, offering a way to rule out background interference for dark matter searches, the capabilities of detectors, and geoneutrino studies, as well as providing a way to verify theoretical predictions regarding sky maps for particle astronomy, such as those related to dark matter annihilation or decay in local sources. This research demonstrates that being able to measure nuclear recoil directions within a plane perpendicular to an experiment's axis offers the potential to access 3D information, thereby providing access to redden sky maps, such as those related to dark matter signals. This is particularly true for experiments with a vertical axis, like DAEδALYSS, which offers the potential to measure recoil directions, even with a small target mass, a deep location, and a single plane of polarization, offering the possibility of detecting dark matter particles with a mass of up to 0.5 GeV. This is particularly true when searching for WIMP particles interacting with a nuclear cross-section of up to 0.1 pb, particularly when utilizing a target mass of just 0.35 g, a target of copper, and a total exposure of 0.35 g d. A comprehensive understanding of commercial driving behavior is vital for developing effective strategies to minimize accidents and enhance road safety. Despite significant research, current methods primarily rely on self-reporting, which often overlooks crucial external factors such as weather, road conditions, and time of day. In this paper, we introduce a system that empowers truck drivers to log and analyze their driving behavior using a mobile application and a real-time notification system. This proposed system is being implemented and tested through the collection of actual driving data from a substantial number of truck drivers over an extended period. Our initial findings, involving 1,000 drivers and nearly 1.5 million miles of driving, highlight the crucial role of location, weather, and road conditions in shaping commercial driving behavior.

To translate an image into machine-readable text, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems employ a two-stage process, consisting of an text detection and recognition stage. Deep neural network-based OCR models have made significant progress in the well-known characters, but they still struggle with variability in scene text instances not encountered during training, such as diverse fonts, styles, and layouts. This paper introduces a character-centric OCR system, which treats character detection and recognition separately, then merges the detected character positions. It then utilizes a recognition model to handle multiple detected characters, regardless of their order, effectively decoupling the two stages. The proposed character-based OCR system was tested with existing detection models and a novel recognition model, and the results demonstrate improved performance and feature representation, and potential for enhanced text detection models when combined with existing recognition models, especially in handling unseen character sets.
